check:0:0.q: Why not “The test set was too small”?
check:0:0.a:
"The test set was too small" has a grain of truth. A small test set does make it more likely that a rare group slips through. With 15 refund-fraud questions out of 300, that group is only 5% of the data. A random split can easily hand the test set zero of them.

But size isn't the real cause. Even a bigger test set could still end up with no fraud questions by bad luck. Growing it only lowers the odds. It also takes examples away from dev, the set you tune prompts against. The real problem is that nothing in the split *guaranteed* every group shows up.

Stratifying fixes that at any size. "Stratify" means you first sort examples by group, then deal each group across the sets on purpose, like dealing cards from a separate deck. The 15 fraud questions would go 9 to dev, 3 to test and 3 to holdout. Every set gets some, every time.

"The split wasn't stratified, so a small group could miss a set entirely" is better because it names the actual cause and points straight to the fix.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Refund fraud questions are too hard to evaluate”?
check:0:1.a:
That option points at the questions, but the problem is in how they were split.

**What it gets right:** refund-fraud questions may well be tricky. They likely behave differently from ordinary questions. That instinct is useful, because a group that behaves differently is exactly the kind you should split by.

**What it misses:** how hard a question is has no effect on where a random split puts it. A random split ignores what each example is about. With only 15 fraud questions out of 300, a 20% test set should get about 3 of them. But nothing guarantees that, and by plain bad luck it can get zero. Easy questions would have the same risk if there were only 15 of them.

It also hints at the wrong fix. "Too hard to evaluate" suggests dropping them. Hard groups are the ones you most need in your test set.

**Why the right answer is better:** "The split wasn't stratified, so a small group could miss a set entirely" names the real cause. Stratifying means dealing each group across dev, test and holdout on purpose, so every set gets its share of fraud questions.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that hard groups are the ones you most need in the test set goes beyond the lesson, but it doesn't contradict it. The answer is also close to the 200-word limit.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Nothing, more checks find more bugs”?
check:1:0.a:
It gets one thing right. Looking at results often really does surface problems. That's exactly why the **dev** set exists: check it as often as you like.

What it misses is what the **test** set is *for*. Its job is to tell you how your app will do on questions it has never been shaped around. That only works if your choices weren't guided by it.

When you check the test set after every change and keep whatever scores higher, the test set quietly becomes part of your tuning. Over a week, your prompt drifts toward those specific examples. The score climbs, but some of that climb is the prompt fitting those exact questions, not getting better at real traffic. It's like a student who sees the exam after every practice session. Their marks go up, but the marks stop telling you what they actually know.

So the extra checks don't find more bugs. They wear out your honest measure.

"You're tuning against the test set" is better because it names the real problem: the test set has turned into a second dev set, so it can no longer give you an unbiased score before a release.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The test set is too small to use”?
check:1:2.a:
"The test set is too small to use" has a grain of truth. A small test set gives shaky scores. A few lucky or unlucky examples can swing the number a lot. And the smaller it is, the faster you can accidentally fit your prompt to it.

But the question never says the test set is small. And size isn't the real problem here.

The problem is *how* it's being used. Checking the test set after every change, then tweaking based on what you saw, means you're quietly shaping your prompt to those exact examples. Its score stops telling you how the app does on new questions. It only tells you how well you've learned that one set.

That would happen with a huge test set too. Making it bigger doesn't fix the habit. The fix is to iterate on the **dev** set, which is the one meant for frequent looks. Then check the test set rarely, before a release.

"You're tuning against the test set" is better because it names the actual mistake: the test set has been turned into a second dev set, so it can no longer give an honest score.

judge.notes: No major problems. The claims about small test sets being noisy and easier to overfit come from general knowledge, not the lesson, but they don't contradict it. Length is just under 200 words.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Write another 100 questions by hand”?
check:2:0.a:
Writing another 100 questions by hand does get something right. You'd have more examples, and checking each one yourself means the correct answers are reliable. That is exactly what a **golden** set is: a fixed set you checked by hand.

But it doesn't fix the real problem. All 200 questions would come from the same place: your own head. You'd write them in your style, about the topics you expect, with the same blind spots as the first 100. Real users don't ask like that. They make typos, mix two questions into one, ask about things you never thought of, and their interests change over time. Last year's guesses, doubled, are still guesses.

It also misses **past failures**, the questions your app has actually gotten wrong before. Those are the cases you most want to catch if they ever come back, and you can't invent them from imagination.

"Add real traffic and past failures" is better because it fills the eval set with how people really use the app today, including the spots where it has already broken.

judge.notes: No real problems; the details about typos and shifting interests go slightly beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Ask a model to make up more questions”?
check:2:1.a:
Asking a model to write more questions does get one thing right. It gives you more examples, quickly and cheaply. That can help fill a thin group, like questions that can't be answered.

But the question asks what makes the set **closer to how the app is really used**. Made-up questions don't do that. A model writes questions the way it imagines people ask. Those tend to be tidy, well-phrased and on familiar topics. Real users type half-sentences, make typos, mix two questions together, and ask about things that didn't exist last year.

Made-up questions also share your blind spots. If you prompt a model using your old 100 questions, you mostly get variations of those same 100. The set grows bigger, but not more realistic.

And they can't include the cases where your app actually broke. Only your own logs know those.

"Add real traffic and past failures" is better because it pulls in how people really ask today, plus the exact mistakes you never want to repeat.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “A counter per group” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "If I split an eval set purely at random, a small group, like refund questions, can end up missing from the test set. Then my test score says nothing about refunds."

*The idea:* "So I deal each group separately, like cards from its own deck. I keep a running count for every group. Each new example looks at its group's count and takes the next slot in a fixed pattern: three to dev, one to test, one to holdout. Then the pattern repeats. Every set gets every group in the same proportions."

*An edge case:* "The pattern is fixed, so the input must be shuffled first. Otherwise the order of the data decides the split. Also, a group with fewer than five examples never fills the pattern, so it may get no test or holdout examples at all."

**A likely follow-up**

"What if several questions come from the same user?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* Deal whole bundles instead of single examples. Keep one user's questions together and send the whole bundle to one set. That follows the leakage rule. Leakage means the same information showing up in more than one set, which makes test scores look better than they really are.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs in your numbers**

- **Test matches dev too closely.** A small drop from dev to test is normal. If test is just as high, the same user or document may sit in both sets. That is leakage: test answers seeping in from examples you tuned on.
- **The score is great, then real use is worse.** The test or holdout set has stopped being honest. Someone tuned against it, or peeked at the holdout and changed things.
- **Test climbs steadily each release** while real-world feedback stays flat. That often means people are tuning against test.
- **A group's score is missing, or jumps wildly between runs.** That group probably has zero or one or two examples in that set. A plain random split does this to small groups.
- **Scores can't be compared over time.** Nobody recorded which version, like `faq-v4`, was used.

**Quickest check**

Make a small table. Put groups down the side and dev, test and holdout across the top, then count the examples in each cell. Each row should have roughly the same proportions.

Then list the user and document IDs in each set. No ID should appear in more than one set.

judge.notes: Passes, though the 'small drop from dev to test is normal' claim goes slightly beyond the lesson, and at about 195 words it is right at the length limit.

learn:stops.a:
**Tiny groups.** The 3-1-1 pattern needs at least five examples in a group before every set gets a share. A group with only two examples lands entirely in dev, so test and holdout never see it. Write more examples for rare groups first, or merge them into a similar group.

**Traffic that changes over time.** Real questions drift as products, prices and policies change. A split built months ago can miss what users ask today. Add fresh traffic as a new named version, like `faq-v5`. Keep scoring the old version too, so you can still compare results.

**Examples that must stay together.** Say one user asked three billing questions. Dealing them one at a time spreads them across dev, test and holdout. That is leakage: the test quietly contains something very close to what you tuned on, so scores look better than they really are. Deal whole bundles (all of one user, or all questions about one document) instead of single examples. Then check that each set still has roughly the same mix of groups.

learn:term.q: How is “golden” different from “recent real traffic”?
learn:term.a:
**Golden** examples are a fixed set you checked by hand. "Fixed" means the set stays the same from one run to the next. "Checked by hand" means a person looked over each example. Because it doesn't move, it gives you a steady yardstick.

**Recent real traffic** is a sample of what users have actually been sending lately. "Traffic" just means the requests coming into your app. "Sample" means you take some of them, not all. This part changes over time, because what users ask changes.

So golden is steady and trusted. Recent traffic is fresh and keeps you close to real use.

Think of a cooking school. The golden set is the classic recipes every student is graded on. Recent traffic is what diners actually ordered this week.

They work together. In the lesson's example, billing, shipping and refunds questions can come from both places, plus past failures. Then you stratify: you deal each group across dev, test and holdout. Naming each version, like `faq-v4`, keeps results comparable as the mix changes.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The new version is clearly better, so ship it”?
check:0:0.a:
"Ship it" gets one thing right. The count does favour the new version. Three more questions passed, and counting the disagreements is how you decide a comparison.

What it misses is the reading. You changed the **reranker**, the step that reorders retrieved documents so the best ones come first. So the improvements should trace back to documents. You would expect causes like "moved the right doc up."

Instead, every improvement says "answer is shorter." A reranker has no direct reason to make answers shorter. When every win shares a cause unrelated to your change, the win may not be real. It may come from how you measured.

The likely culprit is the **scorer**, the code or model that grades each answer. If it quietly prefers short answers, it rewards brevity rather than correctness. Shipping now could mean shipping a version that is only better at pleasing a biased grader.

"The scorer may be rewarding short answers" is better because it notices that the cause doesn't match the change, and it points you to check the measurement before trusting the result.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Nothing, causes do not matter once the count is…”?
check:0:2.a:
**What it gets right:** Counting the disagreements is how the lesson decides which version wins. That is the job of McNemar's test, from the Experiment design module.

**What it misses:** The count tells you *which* version scored better. It does not tell you *why*. The "why" comes from reading the traces. And here, the "why" looks wrong.

A reranker reorders retrieved documents. It is the step that decides which documents go to the top. It has no obvious reason to make answers shorter. So when every improvement shares the cause "answer is shorter", that cause has nothing to do with the change you made. The lesson says this is the moment to suspect the measurement itself. A **scorer** is the thing that marks each answer right or wrong. If the scorer favours short answers, the +3 may come from the scorer, not the reranker.

Ignoring the causes means you could ship a change that did not help.

**Why the other option is better:** "The scorer may be rewarding short answers" uses the causes as a warning sign and checks the measurement before trusting the +3.

check:1:0.q: Why not “The ones with the same result”?
check:1:0.a:
It's a natural pick, because those questions are the majority. With 200 questions, maybe 180 land the same way in both versions. It feels like the bulk of the evidence.

There is a small grain of truth in it. Same-result questions tell you the change didn't break those cases. A question both versions fail, like `charged-twice`, may also point to a weakness worth fixing later.

But they can't explain *this* change. If both versions got a question right, or both got it wrong, the change made no difference to the score there. Reading those traces is like studying two photos that look the same to find what moved. You'd spend most of your time on questions that say nothing about why the scores differ.

That's also why McNemar's test (the counting test from Experiment design) ignores them. Only the disagreements count toward the result.

"The ones where the versions differ" is better because those regressions and improvements are the only questions where the change actually altered the outcome, so their traces show what it did.

judge.notes: No significant problems. The claim that same-result questions 'didn't break those cases' is slightly loose for questions both versions fail, but it doesn't contradict the lesson.

check:1:1.q: Why not “A random handful from all 200”?
check:1:1.a:
A random handful does get one thing right. Reading real traces is how you learn what happened. Picking at random also stops you from choosing only the examples that support what you hoped to see.

The problem is where those random picks land. Most of the 200 questions got the same result from both versions. Both right, or both wrong. On those, the change made no visible difference to the outcome, so they can't show you what the change did.

Say only 8 of the 200 questions differ. A random 10 would include, on average, less than one of them. You could read every trace carefully and still find nothing that explains the change.

The questions where the versions disagree are called **discordant pairs**. They are regressions (old right, new wrong) and improvements (old wrong, new right). Every one of them is a case where the change flipped the result. That makes each one worth a side-by-side trace comparison.

"The ones where the versions differ" is the better answer because those are the only questions where the change actually changed something, so every trace you read can teach you something.

judge.notes: Minor: it slightly overclaims that the change caused every flip (the lesson says to suspect the measurement if causes are unrelated), and the point about random picks avoiding cherry-picking is not in the lesson. Neither contradicts it, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

check:2:1.q: Why not “The step that took the longest”?
check:2:1.a:
"The step that took the longest" sounds sensible, because slow steps often matter. But it answers a different question. Timing tells you about speed, which is called **latency**. A regression is about the *answer* going wrong. A step can be slow and still return exactly the same documents in both versions.

It does get one thing right: it makes you look inside the trace, step by step, instead of only at the final answer. That habit is good.

What it misses is the comparison. The slowest step might be slow in both the old and new traces. Then it tells you nothing about what changed. Also, once two traces split apart, every later step can look different too. Those later differences are often just knock-on effects, like dominoes falling.

So you scan both traces from the top. You look for the first step where they stop matching: different documents retrieved, a different order, a different tool, an extra loop.

**"The first step where they differ" is better because everything before it is identical, so that step is where the change actually took effect and caused the different result.**

check:2:2.q: Why not “The final answer's word count”?
check:2:2.a:
Word count is not useless. If the new answer is much shorter or longer, that is a real difference you can see. It can even hint at a measurement problem. The lesson warns about a scorer (the code that grades answers) that likes short answers. If every improvement is simply a shorter answer, word count would help you notice that.

But word count only looks at the very end of the trace. A trace is the step-by-step record of what the agent did. By the final answer, the real cause has already happened. Maybe the reranker pushed a policy document to the top. Maybe a different tool was called. Maybe there was an extra loop. A shorter answer is a symptom, not a reason. It tells you nothing about what to fix.

It is also too general to tally. "Answer got shorter" could come from many different causes. You could not group regressions into a clear pattern like "pushed worse doc up."

"The first step where they differ" is better because it points straight at the moment the two versions split, which is where the cause lives.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Find what changed, count the causes” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "When I compare two versions on the same questions, one overall score hides what changed. Most questions get the same result both times, so they tell me nothing."

*The idea.* "I focus on the questions where the versions disagree. A regression is one the new version gets wrong but the old got right. An improvement is the reverse. For each one, I open both traces, the step-by-step records of a run. I find the first step that differs and label the cause in a few words. Then I count the causes in each direction. That shows what the change did and what to fix next."

*The edge case.* "If every improvement shares a cause unrelated to my change, I suspect the measurement. For example, the scorer might just like short answers."

**Likely follow-up**

"Why not just compare overall accuracy?"

*Hint:* Two versions can tie on accuracy yet disagree on many questions, with gains cancelling losses. Counting the disagreements decides whether the change is real. That is McNemar's test, which looks only at those questions. Reading them explains why.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **You only have one number.** The report says "score went from 70% to 72%" and nothing else. That small gain could hide 10 improvements and 8 regressions. The regressions are questions that now break, and nobody knows why.
- **The causes are vague.** Labels like "model did better" or "random" mean nobody opened the traces. A trace is the step-by-step record of one run. A good cause names a step: "retrieved the wrong doc", "called the wrong tool".
- **The causes don't touch your change.** You changed the reranker, but every improvement is "answer got shorter". That points to the scorer, not your change. A scorer that likes short answers can make a version look better when it isn't.
- **Surprises in real use.** Users hit failures on the same kinds of questions that regressed, because those were never read.

**Quickest check**

Pick two or three questions that flipped. Open the old and new traces side by side. Find the first step where they differ. If that step has nothing to do with what you changed, distrust the result.

Also check the arithmetic: improvements minus regressions should equal the change in the number of questions passed.

judge.notes: No clear problems. The answer matches the lesson, stays under 200 words, and gives no solution code. 'Reranker' and 'scorer' are used without a definition, which is a minor risk for beginners.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The answers are random from run to run.** LLMs can give a different answer to the same question even when nothing changed. Some "regressions" are then just noise, not caused by your change. Run each version several times on each question. Only count a question as a regression or improvement if it flips the same way every time.

**2. There are very few disagreements.** With only two or three discordant pairs, a pattern like "mostly moved the right doc up" is a guess, not a finding. Treat the labels as hints. Add more questions before you decide what to fix.

**3. There are too many to read, or the traces are long.** A big agent might take twenty steps per question. It might also disagree on hundreds of questions. Reading every pair by hand stops being practical. Read a random sample instead, say thirty pairs. Alternatively, let an LLM draft the cause labels and check a portion of them yourself.

learn:term.a:
"Disagree" is the bigger group. "Regression" is one kind inside it.

**Disagree** means the two versions got different results on the same question. One was right, the other was wrong. Statisticians call these **discordant pairs**, which just means "pairs that don't match."

A disagreement can go two ways:
- **Regression**: the old version was right and the new one is wrong. The change broke something.
- **Improvement**: the old version was wrong and the new one is right. The change fixed something.

So every regression is a disagreement, but not every disagreement is a regression.

An everyday comparison: you retake a quiz. The questions you answered differently are your disagreements. Some you got wrong this time after getting them right before. Those are regressions. Others you newly got right. Those are improvements.

In the lesson's example, three questions disagree:
- `return-label` and `refund-time` are improvements.
- `change-address` is a regression.
- `charged-twice` failed in both versions, so it's not a disagreement and gets skipped.

They work together like this. First you find the disagreements. Then the direction of each one tells you whether to call it a regression or an improvement. Then you label why it changed.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Four of those tickets needed no work to close”?
check:0:0.a:
That answer does notice something real: those 4 passes are strange, and something needs explaining.

But the question rules it out. Every task asks the agent to close an **open** ticket. So no ticket started out closed. And the do-nothing agent changes nothing. After its run, all 10 tickets are still open. None of them got "closed for free."

So the 4 passes can't come from the tickets. They come from the **checker**, the part that marks each run pass or fail. The do-nothing agent is a **no-op baseline**: a test agent that must score 0. If it passes even one run, the checker has a bug.

Blaming the tickets is risky. It shifts the fault onto the tasks, so you'd go "fixing" your eval data while the broken checker keeps passing false successes.

The likely cause is a judge that reads only the reply. It sees "Done!" and believes it. A code check like `ticket_closed`, which reads the real ticket status, would fail all 10 runs.

"The checker trusts the reply instead of the ticket" is better because it names the real fault: the checker grades the agent's claim, not the actual end state.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The real agent only has to beat 4 out of 10”?
check:0:2.a:
That answer treats 4 out of 10 as a fair starting bar, like a score to beat. It does get one thing right: comparing against a simple baseline (a plain reference agent) is a good habit.

But here the baseline should not score anything. Every task is "close an open ticket." The do-nothing agent closes nothing, so its true score is 0 out of 10. If it passes 4 runs, those 4 passes are wrong. That is not a bar for the agent. It is evidence of a bug in the checker.

And a broken checker breaks every score it gives. If it passed "Done!" on a still-open ticket, it can pass the real agent's false successes too. Those are runs where the agent claims it closed the ticket but didn't. So "beating 4" could still hide many failures. You can't trust the real agent's number until the checker is fixed.

"The checker trusts the reply instead of the ticket" is better because it names the actual fault: the checker reads what the agent says, not the ticket's real status. That points straight to the fix, a code check that reads the ticket table.

check:1:0.q: Why not “A judge with a friendlier rubric”?
check:1:0.a:
A **rubric** is the set of instructions a judge uses to decide pass or fail. A "friendlier" rubric is a more lenient one, so it lets more runs pass.

That is the opposite of what you need here. The judge already passed a run it should have failed. Being kinder means it would pass that run again, plus others it might have caught before. You would get fewer real catches, not more.

The deeper problem is what the judge looks at. It reads only the reply. The reply says "I've refunded the order", and that sounds like success. No wording in the rubric can reveal that the refund never happened, because that fact isn't in the reply at all. A stricter rubric wouldn't fully fix it either. A confident false claim still reads like a real one.

So this option gets nothing right for this problem. It changes how the judge grades, but not what the judge can see.

"A code check that reads the refund record" is the right answer. It checks the real end state in the system, so a false claim in the reply can't fool it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Asking the agent to check itself”?
check:1:1.a:
Asking the agent to check itself sounds sensible. It does get one thing right: something should double-check the claim before you trust it.

The problem is *who* is checking. The agent is the one that just said "I've refunded the order" when it hadn't. Whatever went wrong the first time can easily go wrong again. Maybe it misread a tool result, or it assumed the step worked. So it will likely confirm its own claim.

It also has the same blind spot as your judge. It is still working from its own words and beliefs, not from the real world. A confident "yes, it's done" from the agent is just another reply. That is exactly what fooled the judge.

Think of a student marking their own exam. If they thought the wrong answer was right, they'll mark it right.

**A code check that reads the refund record is better because it looks at the actual end state, the real record in the system, so a false claim can't talk its way past it.**

check:2:0.q: Why not “6, the mistakes it caught”?
check:2:0.a:
The number 6 is real, and it matters. It's how many planted mistakes the checker caught. That count tells you about its **recall**: how many of the faults it found. Here it found 6 of the 10, so it missed 4.

But the question asks about **false alarms**. A false alarm is a good run, one with nothing planted, that the checker failed by mistake. The 6 caught runs aren't mistakes by the checker. They're exactly what it should flag.

Think of hiding 10 errors in an essay. The proofreader circles 6 of them. That's good work. They also circle 2 sentences that were fine. Those 2 are the false alarms.

So you look at two lists, two ways:
- Go through the planted runs and ask "was it flagged?" Yes is a catch (6), no is a miss (4).
- Go through the flagged runs and ask "was it planted?" No is a false alarm (2).

"2, the good runs it flagged" is right because false alarms count only good runs the checker wrongly failed, never the real mistakes it caught.

check:2:2.q: Why not “4, the mistakes it missed”?
check:2:2.a:
The number 4 is real. It just answers a different question.

You planted 10 mistakes and the checker flagged 6 of them. So 4 planted mistakes slipped through. Those are **misses**: bad runs the checker passed. Counting them matters, because misses are how a weak checker hides. Too many misses means low **recall** (the share of planted mistakes it caught, here 6 of 10).

But a **false alarm** is the opposite kind of error. It is a good run, with nothing planted, that the checker failed anyway. Misses come from the planted list. False alarms come from the flagged list.

Think of the two lists from the lesson:

- Walk through the planted runs: flagged means a catch, not flagged means a miss. That gives 6 caught and 4 missed.
- Walk through the flagged runs: not planted means a false alarm. That gives 2.

So "4" mixes up the two kinds of error.

"2, the good runs it flagged" is right because a false alarm means failing a run that had no planted mistake, and exactly 2 such runs were flagged.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Check the real end state, not the claim” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
An agent's reply is just words. It can say "I've closed the ticket" even when its tool call failed, or when it never made the call at all. Words cost nothing. The real result lives somewhere else: in the ticket table.

A judge that reads only the reply has no way to tell the difference. A confident "Done!" looks the same whether the work happened or not. So the judge passes it.

Here is what that looks like in real work. Say your support agent handles 200 tickets overnight. Its tool for closing tickets breaks after an update. Every reply still says "Closed it for you!" Your judge scores 100% pass. Your dashboard looks great. Meanwhile 200 customers are still waiting, and you only find out when complaints arrive.

A code check avoids this. It looks up the ticket and asks one plain question: is `status` equal to `"closed"`? That is what `ticket_closed` does in the lesson. It ignores what the agent claims and reads what actually changed.

The do-nothing agent is the quick test. It changes nothing and says "Done!". If your checker passes it, the checker is trusting words, not results.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Compare two lists both ways” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem.** A checker that misses mistakes looks just like one that works, because every run passes. So I plant mistakes on purpose and see what the checker flags. Flagged means marked as failing.

**The idea.** I compare two lists: the planted ids and the flagged ids. I check them both ways. First I walk through the planted list and ask, "Was this one flagged?" Yes is a catch. No is a miss. Then I walk through the flagged list and ask, "Was this one planted?" A no there is a false alarm, a good run failed by mistake.

**The trade-off.** You need both directions. A checker that flags every run catches every planted mistake, so it looks perfect if you only check one way. The second pass shows its false alarms.

**A likely follow-up**

*"What if no mistakes were planted at all?"*

Hint for a strong answer: "caught 0 of 0" means you cannot work out a catch rate (its recall). Report it as unknown, not as perfect. Then point out that this is why every test set should include planted faults, like the do-nothing agent.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs your checker is fooling you**

- **The pass rate is almost perfect, run after run.** Real agents slip up. A checker that never fails anything may simply not be looking.
- **Scores look great in testing, then drop in real use.** Users report tickets still open, while your results said "resolved".
- **Short, confident replies score as well as detailed ones.** If "Done!" passes as often as a real fix, the judge is grading the tone of the reply, not the result.
- **Your two checkers disagree.** In the results table, the judge's `resolved` column says pass, but `ticket_closed` says fail. That gap is usually a false success: the agent claimed it finished, but nothing changed.
- **Traces show no real work.** A trace is the step-by-step log of what the agent did. If it shows no tool call that updated the ticket, yet the run passed, something is wrong.

**The quickest check**

Run the do-nothing agent through your checker. It changes nothing and just says "Done!". It must score 0. If even one of its runs passes, your checker has a bug. Then plant a few false successes and confirm each one gets flagged.

learn:stops.a:
Planted mistakes work well, but here are three places they need extra care.

**Real mistakes don't look like yours.** Your checker can catch every fault you planted and still miss the kinds you never thought of. Also review a sample of real runs by hand, and turn each new failure you find into another planted case.

**Too few planted runs.** "Caught 1 of 3" tells you very little, because one lucky catch swings the number a lot. Plant several runs of each fault type, so recall (the share of planted mistakes caught) means something.

**The end state is hard to read.** A code-based grader needs a reliable place to check, like the ticket table. Sometimes the agent's action leaves no table to read, such as sending an email, or another process changes the ticket after the run. Run tests in a sandbox (a safe copy of your systems) and record the state right after each run. When there is no state to read, give the judge the trace (the log of every tool the agent called) instead of only the final reply.

judge.notes: No blocking problems; the third item runs to four sentences, slightly over the two-or-three guideline.

learn:term.a:
**They're the same thing.** In this lesson, "checker" and "grader" are two names for one job: marking each agent run as pass or fail. "Checker" is the plain-words name. "Grader" is what most people in the field call it. MLflow calls it a **scorer**, which is why the code uses `@scorer`.

Think of a teacher marking homework. You could call them the marker or the grader. Same person, same red pen.

The difference that matters is between **kinds** of checkers:

- An **LLM judge** reads the agent's reply and decides if it sounds right. In the code, that's `resolved`.
- A **code-based grader** checks the real result, such as reading the ticket table. That's `ticket_closed`.

In the lesson's example, the judge was fooled by `claim-1`. That run said "done", but the ticket was still open. The judge also passed the do-nothing agent, `idle-1`. The code grader caught both of those. Each one missed something on its own. Run them together, and fail a run if either one flags it. Then all 3 planted mistakes get caught.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The judge is good: 82 in 100 is high agreement”?
check:0:0.a:
The option gets one thing right. The judge really does agree with the humans 82 times in 100. That number is true. This raw share of matching answers is called the **observed agreement**.

What it misses is *why* they agree. Remember the lesson's example. If 9 in 10 answers are good, a judge that never reads anything and just says "pass" 9 times in 10 still matches the humans about 82 times in 100. Both sides say "pass" nearly all the time, so they line up by luck. A high count can come from a judge that is doing no real work.

That is the gap kappa fills. It takes away the agreement you would expect from luck alone and keeps only what is left. Here kappa is 0.05. That is very close to 0, and 0 means "no better than guessing." So almost all of those 82 matches are luck, not skill.

"The judge is barely better than guessing" is the better answer because it reads the kappa of 0.05, which strips out luck, instead of trusting the raw 82 in 100, which does not.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Kappa must be wrong when agreement is high”?
check:0:1.a:
It's a fair instinct. High agreement next to a tiny kappa looks like a contradiction, and a quick sanity check of your numbers never hurts. That's the part it gets right.

But here, kappa is doing exactly its job. It isn't broken.

Remember the lesson's example. If 9 in 10 answers are good, a judge that never reads anything and says "pass" 9 times in 10 at random still agrees with humans about 82 times in 100. Both sides say pass nearly all the time, so they line up by luck.

Kappa takes that luck away. Here, almost all of the 82 is luck, and only a sliver of real skill is left. So a kappa of 0.05 is the honest number. The 82 is the misleading one.

The option "Kappa must be wrong" trusts raw agreement over kappa. That gets it backwards. Kappa exists because raw agreement can fool you.

"The judge is barely better than guessing" is the better answer because a kappa of 0.05 sits just above 0, and 0 means no better than luck.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Judge B, a lower kappa is stricter”?
check:1:0.a:
"Judge B, a lower kappa is stricter" mixes up two different ideas.

Being strict means failing answers more often. Kappa doesn't measure that. It measures how much better than luck a judge agrees with the humans. A strict judge can have a high kappa or a low one. It depends on whether its fails land on the same answers the humans failed.

What the option gets right is small. A lower number does mean something real. But here the meaning is "closer to guessing," not "tougher."

Kappa works like this. Take the gap between chance agreement and perfect agreement. Kappa is the share of that gap the judge actually covers. Judge B, at 0.1, covers only a tenth of it. So its agreement with the humans is barely more than you would expect from luck alone. Judge A, at 0.75, covers three quarters of that gap. That is above the rough "good" line of 0.6.

"Judge A, it agrees well beyond luck" is better because kappa rewards agreement above chance, and A goes much further past chance than B does.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Neither, kappa can't compare them”?
check:1:2.a:
That option has a grain of truth. Kappa is one number, and the lesson says to use it alongside the pass-and-fail check, not instead of it. So you shouldn't trust a judge on kappa alone.

But "can't compare them" goes too far. Here both judges are scored against the **same human labels**. That means they face the same answers and the same mix of passes and fails, so the chance part of the sum is worked out on equal footing. Kappa also sits on a fixed scale: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than luck. Two kappas on that scale, from the same human labels, can be compared directly.

Read the numbers on that scale. Judge B at `0.1` is barely above guessing. Most of its agreement could come from luck, like the "always says pass" judge in the lesson. Judge A at `0.75` clears the rough "good" line of 0.6.

"Judge A, it agrees well beyond luck" is better because, with the same human labels, `0.75` shows real agreement left over after chance is taken away, while `0.1` shows almost none.

check:2:1.q: Why not “No, kappa replaces that check”?
check:2:1.a:
That option gets one thing right. Kappa is a better single number than plain agreement, because it takes away the agreement you would expect from luck. So a kappa of 0.7 does tell you the judge is doing real work.

What it misses is that kappa is still just one number. It blends passes and failures together. It doesn't tell you where the judge's mistakes are.

That matters because failures are usually rare, and they are often the answers you most need the judge to catch. A judge can earn a decent kappa while still letting a worrying share of real failures slip through as "pass." You only see that when you check passes and failures separately. That means asking how often the judge says "fail" when a human said "fail," and how often it says "pass" when a human said "pass."

So the two checks answer different questions. Kappa asks how much better than luck the judge is overall. The pass-and-fail check asks which kind of answer it gets wrong.

"Yes, use both checks together" is better because kappa shows the judge beats luck, while the pass-and-fail check shows whether it catches the failures you care about.

judge.notes: No real problems. The answer is about 200 words, right at the limit. The claim that failures are usually rare goes slightly beyond the lesson, but its 9-in-10-good example supports it.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Only if kappa drops below 0.6”?
check:2:2.a:
**What it gets right:** a kappa below 0.6 is a real warning sign. If kappa drops that low, you should dig in. So the instinct to check is sound.

**What it misses:** kappa is one number for the whole judge. It mixes passes and failures together. A kappa of 0.7 can look healthy while the judge still does badly on one side.

Failures are often the weak side, because they are rare. Say only 1 answer in 10 is a fail. The judge could catch most passes well and miss half the fails. The overall kappa might still look fine. But catching fails is usually the whole point of a judge. Those are the bad answers you want to stop.

Also, 0.6 is only a rough guide, not a hard line. Waiting for a single number to cross it means you might never look at the problem.

**Why "Yes, use both checks together" is better:** kappa tells you the judge beats luck overall, and the pass-and-fail check shows *where* it might still be failing, so you need both to trust it.

judge.notes: No clear problem. The claims that fails are rare and are the point of a judge go slightly beyond the lesson, but they don't contradict it and are framed as 'often' or 'usually'.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Count, then take away luck” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**The 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "Raw agreement can fool you. Say 9 in 10 answers are good. A judge that says 'pass' to nearly everything will still match the humans most of the time. It looks accurate, but it read nothing."

*The idea.* "So I count how often the judge and the humans really agree. Then I work out how often they'd agree by luck alone, based on how often each one says pass. Kappa is how much of the gap between luck and perfect the judge actually closes. 1 is perfect. 0 is no better than luck."

*The trade-off.* "Kappa can look harsh when fails are rare. A few misses on those rare cases drag it down a lot. So I report it next to the pass-and-fail check, not instead of it."

**A likely follow-up**

"What kappa would you need before you trust the judge?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Give the rough guide: above 0.6 is good, above 0.8 is very good. Then say the bar depends on the stakes. A safety check needs a higher bar than a style check. Add that you'd log kappa with `mlflow.log_metric` and check it again whenever the judge's prompt or model changes.

judge.notes: No real problems. The rare-fails caveat, the stakes-dependent bar and the re-check advice go beyond the lesson but do not contradict it. The length is about 200 words, right at the limit.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Agreement looks great, but the judge rarely says fail.** If 95% agreement comes from a judge that says "pass" almost every time, it may just be riding along with your mostly-good answers. Kappa will be low even though agreement is high.
- **Bad answers slip through in real use.** The judge scored well in testing, then users find failures it never flagged. Often only agreement was measured, and luck hid the problem.
- **Kappa near 0, or below 0.** Near 0 means no better than guessing. Below 0 means worse than guessing. That often points to a bug, such as the two lists being in different orders, or pass and fail swapped.
- **Kappa missing or an error.** If every label on both sides is "pass", chance agreement is 1, and the formula divides by zero. You need some fails in your test set.

**Quickest check**

Put two numbers side by side in your MLflow run: plain agreement and `judge_kappa`. A big gap between them means luck is doing the work. Then count how many fails the judge gave, and compare that with how many fails the humans gave.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. Minor: the divide-by-zero point and the claim that a kappa near 0 'often' means a bug go beyond the lesson, though they don't contradict it.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Very lopsided data.** If almost every answer passes, kappa can look low even when the judge agrees on nearly everything. One edge case: if a judge says "pass" on every answer and the humans do not, kappa comes out as 0. That correctly says it is no better than luck. If the humans and the judge both give the same label on every answer, chance agreement is exactly 1. The formula then divides by zero, so kappa has no value. To avoid both problems, gather more failing examples and always read kappa next to the pass-and-fail check.

**2. Very little data.** On ten answers, one changed label can move kappa a lot. Label more answers before trusting it. Aim for dozens, ideally a hundred or more.

**3. Scores instead of pass or fail.** Some judges give a score from 1 to 5. Plain kappa treats a 4-versus-5 mix-up as just as wrong as 1-versus-5. Use **weighted kappa** instead. It is a version that gives partial credit when the two scores are close.

judge.notes: "Both give the same label on every answer" is misleading: if they agree on every answer and the labels are mixed, kappa is 1; the divide-by-zero case happens only when every answer has the same single label.

learn:term.a:
**Cohen's kappa** is a score for how well a judge (here, the model grading answers) agrees with humans, after removing the agreement that would happen by pure luck.

**Everyday comparison:** picture a weather forecaster in a desert who says "sunny" every single day. They'd be right almost always. That sounds great, but they never looked at the sky. Kappa asks: how much of that rightness came from actually looking?

**The scale:** 1 means perfect agreement. 0 means no better than guessing. Below 0 means worse than guessing. As a rough guide, above 0.6 is good and above 0.8 is very good.

**In the lesson's example:** humans and the judge agree on 9 of 10 answers, so observed agreement is 0.90. But both say "pass" most of the time, so they'd agree about 0.74 of the time by chance alone. Kappa looks at the room left above chance (1 − 0.74 = 0.26). Then it asks how much of that room the judge really covered (0.90 − 0.74 = 0.16). That gives about 0.62.

So 90% agreement becomes "good, not great" once luck is taken out.

check:0:1.a:
"The model is wrong" is a natural first guess. The eval said "wrong", so it's easy to blame the model. And sometimes the model really is the problem.

But look at what the model actually said: "Paris." That is the right city. The only differences from "paris" are a capital letter and a full stop. Those are formatting, not meaning.

So the mistake isn't in the model. It's in the scoring. The eval compared the two strings exactly as they were, character by character. To that kind of check, "P" and "p" are different, and the extra "." is an extra character. A correct answer got marked wrong.

Blaming the model here has a real cost. You might rewrite your prompt or switch models to fix a problem that was never there. Your scores would also look worse than your app really is.

"The comparison isn't normalised" is the better answer. It points to the real cause: the answer and the expected answer weren't cleaned the same way (lowercase, punctuation removed, spaces trimmed) before being compared.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The eval set is too small”?
check:0:2.a:
"The eval set is too small" points at a real concern, just not this one.

**What it gets right:** small eval sets are a genuine weakness. With only a few examples, one lucky or unlucky answer can swing your score a lot. So more examples usually make an eval more trustworthy.

**What it misses:** this question is about one specific answer being marked wrong. The model said "Paris." and the expected answer was "paris". That's the right city. Only the capital letter and the full stop differ.

Adding more examples wouldn't fix that. Every time the model answers with a capital letter or a full stop, the strict comparison would still call it wrong. You'd just have a bigger pile of unfair "wrong" marks. The problem is in *how* answers are compared, not in *how many* there are.

**Why "The comparison isn't normalised" is better:** it names the actual cause. The eval compares raw text without first cleaning both sides (making them lowercase, removing punctuation, trimming spaces), so formatting differences get counted as mistakes.

judge.notes: No real problems; the closing 'why normalised is better' part runs to two sentences instead of the requested one, which is minor.

check:1:1.a:
"It counts as right" gets one thing correct. A person reading both answers would say they match. "New York." and "new york" mean the same city, and that is exactly the result a good eval *should* give.

What it misses is that the code doesn't think like a person. It compares the two strings exactly, letter by letter. Here only the model's answer gets cleaned. The expected answer is left as it was.

So the comparison looks like this:

```python
"new york" == "New York."   # False
```

The capital letters and the full stop are still on the expected side. To the computer, `N` and `n` are different characters, and `"."` is an extra character. The strings don't match, so the answer is marked wrong.

This is why the lesson says to clean *both* sides. Cleaning just one side leaves the formatting problem in place. It only moves it to the other side.

"It still counts as wrong" is better because it describes what the code actually does. The uncleaned expected answer keeps its capitals and full stop, so the exact comparison fails.

judge.notes: Passes, but the line 'It only moves it to the other side' is vague and slightly misleading, and the closing explanation runs to two sentences instead of the one requested.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The eval skips that one”?
check:1:2.a:
"The eval skips that one" sounds reasonable. It gets one thing right: something about this pair is off, because only one side was cleaned. But the eval has no rule that says "skip pairs that look messy."

An eval just walks through every pair and compares them. Nothing tells it to set a pair aside. Skipping would need extra code that someone wrote on purpose, and this eval doesn't have it.

So here is what actually happens:

- The model's answer gets cleaned: "new york" stays "new york".
- The expected answer is left alone: it's still "New York."
- The comparison is exact. The capital letters and the full stop don't match.

```python
'new york' == 'New York.'   # False
```

That pair is scored as a miss and pulls the score down, even though the model was right. This kind of quiet error is easy to overlook. It's why the lesson says to clean both sides.

"It still counts as wrong" is better because it describes what the eval really does: it compares the cleaned answer with the uncleaned expected answer, they differ, and the pair is marked wrong.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Exact match against one summary”?
check:2:0.a:
Exact match does get one thing right. It is simple, fast and fully repeatable. For answers with one correct string, like "Paris", it works well, especially after you clean both sides.

Summaries are different. There is no single right string. Two good summaries can say the same thing in completely different words. One might say "Customer asked for a refund on a late order." Another might say "The caller wanted money back because the delivery was delayed." Both are correct, but exact match compares letters, not meaning. So the second one scores as wrong.

That means your score would punish good answers just for using different words. Worse, it could reward a bad summary that happens to copy the expected wording. Cleaning (lowercase, removing punctuation, trimming spaces) doesn't help here. It only fixes formatting, not wording.

So "Exact match against one summary" gives you a number, but not a trustworthy one.

"An LLM judge with a clear rubric" is the right choice. A second model grades each summary against written grading rules, like "mentions the customer's problem" and "states the outcome." That lets it judge meaning instead of exact words.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Count how many words each one has”?
check:2:2.a:
Counting words gets one small thing right. It can flag a summary that is far too long or far too short, and it never mistakes different wording for an error.

But it misses the main job: checking whether the summary is **correct**. Word count says nothing about meaning. Look at these two summaries of the same call:

- "Customer wants a refund for a broken phone." (8 words)
- "Customer loves the phone and wants another one." (8 words)

Both have eight words, so counting would score them the same. Yet the second one gets the call completely wrong.

It also fails in the other direction. Two good summaries can be different lengths and still both be right. So matching word counts tells you very little.

What you need is something that understands meaning. That's where **LLM-as-a-judge** comes in: a second model reads each summary and grades it. It follows a **rubric**, which is a written set of grading rules, such as "mentions the customer's problem" and "states what the agent did."

An LLM judge with a clear rubric is better because it checks whether the summary says the right things, whatever words it uses.

judge.notes: The claim that word counting 'never mistakes different wording for an error' contradicts the later point that good summaries of different lengths would be wrongly scored, and the idea that word count can flag length problems is not from the lesson.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Clean up before comparing answers” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
When a computer compares two pieces of text, it checks them character by character. `"Paris."` and `"paris"` differ in two places: the capital `P` and the full stop. So a correct answer gets marked wrong.

Here's how that bites in real work. Say you tweak your prompt (the instructions you give the model) so it answers in a tidier style. Your eval (your test set) has ten questions. The expected answers are stored in lowercase with no punctuation, like `"paris"`. The new model replies `"Paris."`, `"Tokyo."` and so on. Every answer is right. But a raw comparison scores 0 out of 10, because each reply has a capital letter and a full stop.

Now clean both sides: make them lowercase, remove the marks, and trim spaces. `"Paris."` becomes `"paris"`, which matches. The score is 10 out of 10.

Skip the cleaning, and you might undo a good change because the numbers looked terrible. Or you might pick the worse of two models just because it formats text the way your answer list happens to.

Clean both sides, too. Expected answers are often typed by people, and they can have stray spaces or capitals of their own.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Clean both sides, then compare” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "When I score a model against expected answers, small formatting differences cause false failures. 'Paris.' and 'paris' mean the same thing. A plain text comparison still marks them as different."

*The idea:* "So I clean both sides the same way before comparing. I make the text lowercase, remove punctuation and trim spaces off the ends. Then the score shows whether the answer is right, not how it was typed."

*The trade-off:* "Cleaning can hide real differences. Removing the dot turns '3.5' into '35', which is a different number. So I keep the cleaning rules small and fit them to the task."

**A likely follow-up**

"What if answers are open-ended, so there's no single right string?"

*Hint for a strong answer:* Say that exact matching stops working there. Then explain LLM-as-a-judge. A second model, the judge, grades each answer against a rubric, which is a set of written grading rules. Finish by saying you'd check the judge too. For example, you could compare its grades with human grades on a sample of answers.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs the cleaning step was skipped or done wrong**

- **The score looks too harsh.** Your exact-match number is low, but when you read the answers, most look right. Failures like "Paris." vs "paris" mean formatting is being marked wrong, not content.
- **The score jumps around after tiny prompt changes.** If a new prompt makes the model add a full stop or capital letter, the score drops even though the facts didn't change.
- **Only one side was cleaned.** If you cleaned the model's answer but not the expected answer, a stray space or `?` in your test set still causes misses.
- **The count looks off.** `zip` stops at the shorter list. If you have 50 predictions but 48 answers, two get dropped silently, and the score is based on the wrong number of pairs.
- **A crash on an empty test set.** That means the empty-list check is missing.

**Quickest check**

Pull up five or six answers marked "wrong." Put each prediction next to its expected answer. If the only differences are case, punctuation or spaces, your cleaning isn't working. Also confirm both lists have the same length before scoring.

judge.notes: No real problem. The point that zip stops at the shorter list goes beyond the lesson but is true and does not contradict it. The answer is also close to the 200-word limit.

learn:stops.a:
Exact match after cleaning is a great start, but it has limits.

**1. Open-ended answers from an LLM app.**
A chatbot might say "The capital of France is Paris" when the expected answer is "Paris." Cleaning won't make those strings equal, so a correct answer gets marked wrong. Use LLM-as-a-judge here. A second model grades the answer against a rubric, like MLflow's `Correctness` scorer does.

**2. Cleaning changes the meaning.**
Removing `.` turns "3.5" into "35", which could match a wrong answer. Lowercasing can also hide differences that matter, like product codes. Choose your cleaning rules for each kind of answer. For example, compare numbers as numbers, not as text.

**3. Very few test examples.**
With only five questions, one answer flipping moves your score by 20 points. That can look like a big win or loss when nothing really changed. Add more examples, and read the failures yourself before trusting the number.

judge.notes: No blocking problems. Minor: the answer calls MLflow's Correctness scorer a judge-style scorer, which the lesson doesn't say, and sections 1 and 2 run to four sentences against the two-to-three limit.

learn:term.a:
They're two sides of the same idea. One is the method, the other is the thing doing the work.

**LLM-as-a-judge** is the *approach*. It's a way of scoring answers when there's no single right string to compare against. Instead of checking for an exact match, you ask a model to do the grading.

**The judge** is the *grader itself*. It's the second model, separate from the one answering the questions. It reads each answer and scores it using a **rubric**, which is a set of written grading rules.

How they fit together: LLM-as-a-judge is the plan, and the judge carries it out, guided by the rubric.

An everyday comparison: "peer marking" is a method a school might use. The classmate holding the marking sheet is the one who actually grades your work. The method and the person are related, but they're not the same thing.

In this lesson, "Capital of France?" has one right answer, "Paris". So cleaning both sides and comparing is enough. A judge is for open-ended answers, where many different wordings could be correct. Later lessons cover how to check that the judge itself grades well.

check:0:1.a:
"32" gets one thing right. Bisecting does cut the list in half. After your first check, only 32 versions are still in question.

But 32 is the size of what's left after **one** check, not the number of checks. The halving doesn't stop there. You check the middle of those 32, and now only 16 remain. Then 8, then 4, then 2, then 1.

Count the checks, not the versions:

```
64 -> 32   (check 1)
32 -> 16   (check 2)
16 -> 8    (check 3)
8  -> 4    (check 4)
4  -> 2    (check 5)
2  -> 1    (check 6)
```

So you run about 6 evals, not 32.

Another way "32" can sneak in is by picturing yourself testing versions one by one until you reach the middle. That is still walking through the list in order, just stopping halfway. Bisecting never does that. It jumps straight to the middle every time.

"6" is better because each eval throws away half of what's left, and 64 halves down to 1 in six steps.

check:0:2.a:
"64" is what you'd need if you tested every version one by one, starting from the oldest. That approach does work. You would find the first failing version. So the number isn't silly. It's the cost of the slow, careful way.

What it misses is the pattern in the results. All the passing versions come first, then all the failing ones. That means one check tells you more than "this version is good or bad." It tells you which **half** the problem is in.

So you test the middle and throw away the half that can't contain the change. Each eval cuts what's left in half:

- 64 versions → 32
- 32 → 16
- 16 → 8
- 8 → 4
- 4 → 2
- 2 → 1

That's six checks to land on one version. With MLflow, that's six eval runs instead of sixty-four. That saves real time and money.

**"6" is better because each bisecting check halves the versions still in question, and 64 can only be halved six times before one version is left.**

check:1:0.a:
"Somewhere from 1 to 10" picks the wrong half.

It does get one thing right. Testing version 10 splits the 20 versions into two halves, and the answer is in one of them. That is the core move of bisecting.

But the test result points the other way. Version 10 **passed**. In this setup, all the passing versions come first, then all the failing ones. So if version 10 passes, every version before it passes too. Versions 1 through 10 are all fine. None of them can be the first bad one.

Think of it like a line of green lights followed by red lights. If light 10 is green, the switch to red must happen after it.

Choosing 1 to 10 would also waste money. You would spend more eval runs on versions you already know are good.

"Somewhere from 11 to 20" is better because a pass at version 10 rules out everything up to 10, so the first failure must come later.

check:1:2.a:
"It must be version 20" gets one thing right. Version 20 fails, so it is a bad version. It could even be the first bad one.

But it misses how the versions are laid out. All the passing versions come first, then all the failing ones. Once something breaks, every later version also fails. So a failure at version 20 doesn't mean the break happened at 20. It only means the break happened at 20 or earlier.

Picture this: version 13 introduced the problem. Then versions 13, 14, and so on up to 20 all fail. Version 20 failing looks exactly the same as it would if 20 were the culprit. You can't tell those cases apart yet.

What you do know is this. Version 10 passes, so the break came after 10. Version 20 fails, so the break came at 20 or before. That leaves a range, not a single answer. Your next step in bisecting is to test the middle of that range, around version 15.

"Somewhere from 11 to 20" is better because it states only what the two results actually prove: after the last known pass, and no later than the known fail.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Test only the newest few versions”?
check:2:0.a:
"Test only the newest few versions" gets one thing right: it's cheap. A handful of eval runs costs far less than 50.

But it misses the real question. You already know the newest version is broken. That's why you're looking. Since all the passing versions come first and all the failing ones come after, the newest few will almost surely fail too. Each of those runs just tells you "yes, still broken." You pay for the eval and learn almost nothing.

It only works if the breaking change happened very recently. If the problem started at version 12, testing versions 48, 49 and 50 never gets near it. You'd have spent money and still not know where things went wrong.

"Test the middle, keep the half with the change" is better. Every run throws away half of the remaining versions, wherever the break is. So you're sure to find the first bad version in about 6 runs out of 50.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Test the oldest version first”?
check:2:1.a:
Testing the oldest version first does have one thing going for it. It confirms you have a known-good starting point, a version that really passes. That's a sensible sanity check.

But it barely narrows the search. The oldest version almost always passes, so the result tells you what you already expected. And if you keep going in order (oldest, then the next, then the next), you're walking through the list one version at a time. In the worst case, that's all 50 eval runs. Each one costs money and time.

The problem is that each check only rules out a single version. The other 49 are still in question.

Testing the middle works differently. Say version 25 passes. Then the break must be somewhere in 26 to 50, and you've ruled out 25 versions with one run. Repeat on the remaining half, and you find the first bad version in about 6 runs instead of 50.

**Testing the middle is better because every check throws away half of the remaining versions, not just one.**

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Check the middle, drop half” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "We had 40 prompt versions, and one of them made quality worse. Each eval, meaning a scored test run, costs time and money. Re-running all 40 is wasteful."

*The idea:* "Versions pass up to a point, then fail. So I test the middle one. If it passes, the break is later. If it fails, the break is there or earlier. Each check throws away half of what's left. Forty versions take about 6 evals. A thousand take about 10. In MLflow I log each check as a named run, so the trail is easy to review."

*The edge case:* "This only works if all the passes come before all the fails. If quality bounces up and down, the search can point at the wrong version. And if every version passes, there's nothing to find."

**Likely follow-up**

"What if your eval is flaky, meaning it can give different results on the same version?"

Hint: One wrong result sends the search into the wrong half, and it never comes back. A strong answer is to rerun the middle version a few times, or use a larger eval set with a score threshold, before trusting the result.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs it went wrong**

- **The eval bill or wait time is huge.** You ran all 40 versions when about 6 checks would do. That means bisecting was skipped.
- **The blamed version looks harmless.** Its change has nothing to do with the failure. Your search may have kept the wrong half.
- **You're off by one.** The search named the last passing version, not the first failing one.
- **Results are mixed, not clean.** In MLflow (the tool that logs each eval run) you see pass, fail, pass. Bisecting assumes all passes come first, then all fails. If scores are "flaky", meaning they change when you rerun the same version, bisecting can point anywhere.
- **Runs are hard to match to versions.** Some MLflow runs lack the `prompt_version` tag, so you can't tell what each run tested.

**Quickest check to confirm**

Rerun just two versions: the blamed one and the one right before it. The blamed one should fail. The one before should pass. Run each twice. That shows the result is steady, not luck. If both checks hold, you found the real change.

learn:stops.a:
Bisecting assumes one clean switch: every version before the change passes, every version after fails. Here is where that breaks.

**Noisy LLM scores.** An LLM can answer differently each run, so one eval might "fail" by chance. Bisecting trusts every check, so one fluke sends you to the wrong half. Run each middle version a few times, or use a larger eval set, and decide pass or fail on the average.

**Results that flip back and forth.** Say v12 broke something, v18 fixed it, and v25 broke it again. The pattern is no longer "passes, then fails." Bisecting will find *a* failure, but maybe not the one you care about. Look at the scores across versions first, or bisect each stretch separately.

**The cause isn't in your versions.** A model provider might update their model, or your RAG documents (the files your app searches before answering) might change. Then old versions fail today even though nobody touched them. Bisecting your prompt versions won't find this. Re-run a known good version first. If it now fails too, the problem is outside your code.

learn:term.a:
Here, a **regression** means a change that made things worse. Something that used to work stops working after an update.

**An everyday comparison:** your phone gets an update, and now the camera app crashes. It worked fine before. The update caused a regression. The phone "went backwards."

**Note:** in machine learning you may also hear "linear regression," a way to predict numbers. That's a different meaning. This lesson only means "things got worse."

**In the lesson's example:** you have 40 prompt versions, oldest first. The early ones pass your evals (your tests of answer quality). At some point, one version starts failing, and every version after it fails too. That first failing version is where the regression came in.

The example narrows it down:

- `v20` passes, so the regression came later.
- `v30` fails, so it's somewhere in `v21` to `v30`.

Each version gets its own MLflow run, named like `prompt-v17`. So the results stay labeled, and you can see which version passed or failed.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Yes: 92 in 100 is high enough to trust its scor…”?
check:0:0.a:
It's a fair instinct. 92 in 100 sounds strong, and overall agreement is a real number worth knowing. The problem is what it hides.

Overall agreement mixes passes and failures into one score. If most answers are good, a judge can score high just by saying "pass" to almost everything.

Picture this: humans passed 92 answers and failed 8. A lazy judge passes all 100. It agrees with humans 92 times in 100, the exact score in the question. Yet it caught none of the 8 bad answers. Those bad answers are the bugs you built the judge to find.

So "92 in 100" can't tell a useful judge from a useless one. You need two separate shares:

- **True positive rate (TPR):** of the answers humans passed, how many the judge also passed.
- **True negative rate (TNR):** of the answers humans failed, how many the judge also failed.

The lazy judge above scores 100% TPR but 0% TNR. That zero is the warning sign.

"Not until you check passes and failures separately" is the better answer because only those two separate shares show whether the judge actually catches failures.

check:0:2.q: Why not “No: a judge needs to agree 100 times in 100”?
check:0:2.a:
**What it gets right:** it doesn't trust the 92 blindly. And a perfect 100 in 100 would mean the judge matched humans on every pass and every failure.

**What it misses:** the lesson's point is that a judge is a model, so it can be wrong. Demanding zero mistakes sets a bar almost no judge would meet, and it skips the real question. It also answers "No" without enough information. The 92 alone can't tell you whether this judge is good or bad.

Why not? It depends on where the 8 misses fall. Suppose 92 of the 100 answers are good. A judge that passes everything also scores 92, yet it catches no failures at all. A different judge with 92 could catch most failures and be quite useful. Same overall number, very different judges.

So split the check. Look at the share of human passes the judge also passed. This is the **true positive rate**. Then look at the share of human failures the judge also failed. This is the **true negative rate**.

"Not until you check passes and failures separately" is better because those two shares show what the single 92 hides: whether the judge actually catches bad answers.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that a perfect score is a bar almost no judge would meet goes slightly beyond the lesson, and the answer is right at the edge of the 200-word limit.

check:1:0.q: Why not “It agrees with humans well”?
check:1:0.a:
"It agrees with humans well" is tempting for one reason. If most answers are good and the judge passes them, the judge will match the humans most of the time overall. A single overall score can look high.

But the question isn't about the good answers. It only tells you about the 20 answers humans **failed**. On those, the judge agreed just 2 times out of 20. That's 10%. This number is the **true negative rate**: of the answers humans failed, the share the judge also failed.

So on the side that matters for finding bugs, the judge mostly disagrees with humans. The other 18 bad answers got a pass from the judge. Calling that "agrees well" mixes up the two sides. It lets the easy passes hide the missed failures. That's exactly the trap the lesson warns about.

"It lets most bad answers through" is better because it names what the numbers actually show: on human failures, the judge missed 18 of 20, so it catches very few real problems.

check:1:1.q: Why not “It is too strict on good ones”?
check:1:1.a:
"It is too strict on good ones" points the wrong way, and it talks about answers the question never shows you.

Look at what the question gives you. All 20 answers are ones the humans **failed**. These are the bad answers. So the numbers tell you nothing about good answers. You can't judge strictness on good answers without knowing how the judge treated the answers humans passed.

The direction is also backwards. "Too strict" would mean the judge fails too much. Here it failed only 2 of the 20 bad answers. That means it passed the other 18. That's too lenient, not too strict.

The one thing the option gets right is that it notices the judge disagrees with the humans. But it describes the disagreement on the wrong side and in the wrong direction.

In the lesson's terms, this is the judge's **true negative rate**. That is the share of human failures the judge also failed. Here it is 2 out of 20, which is 10%. That is very low.

"It lets most bad answers through" is better because it matches the numbers exactly: 18 of the 20 bad answers slipped past the judge as passes.

judge.notes: No real problem; the claim that the option 'notices the judge disagrees' is a slightly generous reading, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

check:2:1.q: Why not “A second judge to grade the first one”?
check:2:1.a:
A second judge sounds sensible. It gets one thing right: if the two judges disagree on an answer, that disagreement is a useful hint that something is off.

But a second judge is still a model, so it can be wrong too. Worse, two models often share the same blind spots. They may be trained on similar data, or prompted in similar ways. Both might pass a bad answer, and their agreement would look like proof when it isn't.

There's also a loop problem. If you need a second judge to check the first, who checks the second? You never reach solid ground.

What's missing is **ground truth**, meaning answers you know are right because a careful person decided. Without it, you can't measure how often the judge passes what humans passed (its true positive rate) or fails what humans failed (its true negative rate). That second number is what catches a judge that just passes everything.

"Human labels on some of the same answers" is better because it gives you a trusted reference to measure the judge against, on passes and failures separately.

check:2:2.q: Why not “A longer and stricter grading prompt”?
check:2:2.a:
A longer, stricter grading prompt isn't a bad idea. Clear instructions often help a judge grade better. A "prompt" is just the text you give the model telling it what to do.

But a better prompt is still a guess. You change the wording and *hope* the scores improved. Nothing tells you if they did.

It can also backfire. A stricter prompt might push the judge to fail good answers. Then its **true positive rate** drops. That is the share of human passes the judge also passes. A looser prompt might do the opposite and miss real failures. That lowers its **true negative rate**, the share of human failures it also fails. From the prompt alone, you can't see either problem.

And at 2,000 answers a week, nobody reads every score. A quiet mistake would spread through all of them.

So the prompt is something you tune. It is not proof the judge works.

"Human labels on some of the same answers" is the right choice. It gives you a known-correct answer key, so you can actually measure how often the judge agrees on passes and on failures.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Count passes and fails separately” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

**The problem:** "An LLM judge is a model, so it can be wrong. If most answers are good, a judge that passes everything still looks accurate overall, but it catches no bugs."

**The idea:** "So I compare the judge with human labels on the same answers and score each side separately. Of the answers humans passed, what share did the judge pass? That's the true positive rate. Of the answers humans failed, what share did the judge fail? That's the true negative rate. A pass-everything judge scores 100% on the first and 0% on the second, which exposes it right away."

**The trade-off:** "Failures are often rare. With only two human failures, one disagreement swings the fail share by 50 points. So I make sure the labeled set includes enough real failures before I trust that number."

**A likely follow-up**

*"Which of the two rates matters more?"*

Hint for a strong answer: it depends on the cost of each mistake. If the judge exists to find bugs, the fail side matters most, because a missed failure ships to users. A false alarm only costs a human a second look.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs your judge isn't being checked properly**
