explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Label each answer, then count” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "An agent with memory can keep repeating an old fact after its source has changed. A normal eval won't notice, because nothing changes while it runs."

*The idea:* "So I plant a change on purpose. Say the office moves from Leeds to York. Then I ask a question that depends on it. Each answer gets one label: current, unsure or stale. Then I count what share of answers got each label."

*The trade-off:* "I score strictly. If an answer mentions the old fact, it's stale, even if it also gives the new one, because the user can't tell which is right. The cost is that a correct answer like 'you moved from Silver to Gold' also scores as stale. So I read a few stale answers by hand."

**A likely follow-up**

"How do you know your scoring isn't too easy to pass?"

*Hint:* Mention two checks.

- **A code check:** it reads the memory store directly, to see if the old fact was marked as replaced.
- **Two baselines:** these are simple stand-ins that should score badly.
  - A memory that never updates should fail the changed facts.
  - No memory at all should fail the facts that didn't change.

judge.notes: No real problems. It sits right at the length limit (about 200 words), and 'Mention two checks' followed by a code check plus two baselines is slightly loose.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Almost no stale answers.** If nearly every answer scores current, be suspicious. Often nothing was actually changed, or the scorer is too lenient.
- **Hedged answers scoring well.** An answer like "York, or maybe Leeds" being marked as passing means the judge only checks whether "York" appears. It should count as stale.
- **Grounding scores all pass.** `RetrievalGroundedness` only compares the answer with what the agent looked up. If the agent pulled the old fact from memory, the answer still "passes."
- **The memory store disagrees.** The answers look current, but the store never marked the old fact as replaced. The agent may have got lucky.
- **Real users complain.** The eval looks great, then people report old addresses or old plan levels.

**Quickest check: run the baselines.** A baseline is a simple stand-in to compare against.

- Plug in a memory that never updates. It should fail the changed facts.
- Then try no memory at all. It should fail the unchanged facts.

If either one scores well, your test isn't really testing memory.

Also read a few stale answers by hand. Some may be correct, like "you moved from Silver to Gold," which mentions the old fact on purpose.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The fact can be worded many ways.** Word matching breaks when the new fact shows up as "the York site" or a date written differently, and some correct answers mention the old value on purpose ("you moved from Silver to Gold"). Use an LLM judge (a second model told to grade each answer against clear rules), and still read a sample of the stale ones by hand.

**2. A fact changes more than once.** If the office goes Leeds, then York, then Hull, "old" now means every past value, not just one. List all earlier values as stale, and plant changes at different times so you test old updates as well as fresh ones.

**3. The system is much bigger.** With many users or a shared memory, one user's update can leak into another's answers, or simply get lost. Plant changes for several users, check the memory store for each one, and keep running both baselines (simple stand-ins that should fail) so a lazy scorer still gets caught.

judge.notes: Point 1 says word matching breaks on "the York site", but that text contains "York", so the lesson's substring check would catch it; a better example would be a paraphrase like "the northern office".

learn:term.a:
**Current** means the agent gave the new fact. After the office moved to York, it says "Your office is in York." That is the answer you want.

**Unsure** means the agent gave no fact at all. It says "I can't confirm that." It didn't help, but it didn't mislead you either. That's honest.

The difference is what the user walks away with. With current, they have the right answer. With unsure, they know they still need to check somewhere else. Neither leaves them believing something false. That trap belongs to the third label, **stale**, where the agent hands over the old fact, Leeds.

Think of asking a friend when the shop closes. "It closes at 6 now" is current. "Not sure, they changed the hours recently" is unsure. "It closes at 8" (the old time) is stale. You'd trust that friend again after the first two, but not the third.

So the two work together. Current shows memory updated properly. Unsure shows the agent knows when it doesn't know. A good agent has lots of current, some unsure, and very little stale.

judge.notes: No significant problems; the closing line about 'lots of current, some unsure, very little stale' goes slightly beyond the lesson but does not contradict it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The users are wrong, since the scores say all i…”?
check:0:0.a:
That option takes the eval scores at face value. It does get one thing right: steady scores are real evidence. Your app still answers the eval questions as well as before.

What it misses is what those scores actually measure. The eval set is a snapshot, a fixed list of questions collected at one point in time. A steady score only means the app still handles *those* questions well. It says nothing about questions that weren't in the list.

Meanwhile, real traffic keeps changing. New products, new policies and new kinds of users bring new kinds of questions. If more people now ask about refunds and your eval set is mostly billing, the score can stay flat while real quality drops.

User complaints come straight from production, meaning the live app real people use. So they are fresher evidence than the eval scores. Dismissing them throws away your best warning sign.

"Real questions have drifted away from the eval set" is better because it explains both facts at once: the scores are steady *and* users are unhappy, since the eval set no longer matches what people actually ask.

judge.notes: No real problems. The only mild overreach is calling complaints the "best warning sign", which the lesson doesn't say, but it doesn't contradict the lesson.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The model got worse overnight and the eval miss…”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. Something really is going wrong in production, and the eval did not flag it.

But look at the clue: eval scores are steady. Your eval works by running the model on a fixed set of questions and scoring the answers. If the model itself had gotten worse, it would do worse on those questions too, and the scores would drop. Steady scores tell you the model still handles the eval questions just as well as before.

So the problem is not the model changing. It is the questions changing. Maybe users now ask much more about refunds, or about a product that launched last week. Your eval set is a snapshot, so it has few or none of those questions. The model can struggle with them while the eval keeps reporting good news.

That is why you track the category mix of real traffic against the eval set. When the gap grows, the eval needs refreshing.

"Real questions have drifted away from the eval set" is better because it explains both clues at once: steady scores *and* more complaints.

judge.notes: No major problem. The claim that the problem is not the model changing is slightly strong, but it follows from the steady-scores clue and is consistent with the lesson.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Keep it, so old scores stay comparable”?
check:1:1.a:
"Keep it, so old scores stay comparable" gets one thing right. If you never change the eval set, this month's score and last month's score are measured the same way. That consistency feels safe.

But it misses the bigger problem. Your eval set is a snapshot from before the launch. Now lots of real questions are about the new product, and the eval set has none of them. The mix of production traffic has moved away from the eval set. That is **drift**: the real questions no longer look like your test questions.

When drift happens, eval scores stop predicting real quality. Your agent could score well on the old questions while giving poor answers about the new product. You would have comparable numbers, but they would be measuring the wrong thing. A steady score that no longer reflects what users ask can hide real failures.

"Refresh the eval set with new questions" is better because it brings the eval set's mix back in line with what users actually ask, so its scores predict real quality again.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Raise the pass mark on the old set”?
check:1:2.a:
Raising the pass mark has one good instinct. It shows you want to be more careful now that things have changed. Being stricter is not a bad idea on its own.

But it doesn't touch the real problem. Your eval set was built before the new product existed. So it has no questions about that product. A higher pass mark still only tests the old kinds of questions. Your agent could ace them and still give poor answers about the new product. You would never see it.

This is **drift**: the mix of real questions has moved away from your eval set. Once that happens, eval scores stop predicting real quality. Making the test harder doesn't help if the test is about the wrong things. It's like making a driving test stricter on city streets when your drivers now mostly use the motorway.

"Refresh the eval set with new questions" is better because it brings the test back in line with what real users ask, so the scores mean something again.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Real traffic is completely different”?
check:2:0.a:
"Real traffic is completely different" mixes up the two ends of the scale.

Total variation distance runs from 0 to 1. To get it, you turn both lists into shares, add up the gap for each category, and halve the total. A result of 1 means the mixes have nothing in common. A result of 0 means every gap is zero.

So this option gets one thing right: the scale has an end that means "completely different." But that end is 1, not 0.

Think about what a 0 needs. For the total to be 0, every single gap must be 0. Since a gap is never negative, nothing can cancel out. Billing's share in production equals billing's share in the eval set. The same goes for shipping, and for refunds. That is the opposite of "completely different."

It also means your eval scores are still a good guide to real quality. Nothing has shifted, so the eval set does not need refreshing yet.

"Real traffic matches the eval set's mix" is the right answer, because a distance of 0 means every category has the same share in both.

check:2:2.q: Why not “The eval set has no questions in it”?
check:2:2.a:
It's natural to read a 0 as "nothing there." But here, the 0 isn't counting questions. It's measuring a **gap**, meaning how far apart two mixes are.

Recall how the number is built. You turn each list of counts into **shares**, meaning each category's slice of its own total. You add up the gap for each category, then halve it. The result is 0 only when every gap is 0. That happens when both lists split their questions the same way.

An empty eval set wouldn't give you 0 at all. With no questions, the total is zero. You can't turn counts into shares, because you'd be dividing by zero. So the measure can't even be worked out. It certainly doesn't land neatly on 0.

That option also misses the point of drift monitoring. The whole idea is comparing two mixes. A 0 is the good news: your eval set still looks like the real world.

"Real traffic matches the eval set's mix" is better because a total variation distance of 0 means every category's share is identical in both lists.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Compare shares, add up the gaps” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "An eval set is a snapshot. Real questions change: new products, new policies, new users. When the mix moves, my eval scores stop predicting how the agent really does."

*The idea.* "So I compare the two mixes. I turn each into shares, so a small eval set and huge production traffic sit on the same scale. I add up the gap for each category and halve it. That's total variation distance. 0 means the same mix. 1 means completely different."

*The trade-off.* "It's one number, so it tells me *that* something moved, not *what*. Next I'd look at the gap for each category. Also, with little traffic the shares jump around. So I wouldn't raise an alarm off one quiet day."

**Likely follow-up:** "What if production has a category your eval set doesn't have at all?"

*Hint:* That's the riskiest drift, because you have no eval coverage there. Its whole production share counts as gap, so the score rises. A strong answer adds: flag brand-new categories on their own, then add examples of them to the eval set.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Signs drift was never checked**

- Your eval scores stay high and steady, but real users complain more. You see more thumbs-down ratings, more handoffs to humans, or more "that's not what I asked" replies.
- Your traces (the logged record of each request) show questions about things your eval set never covers, like a new product or policy.
- An "other" or "uncategorized" bucket keeps growing week after week.

**Signs the measure itself is wrong**

- The distance comes out above 1 or below 0. A correct one always lands between them.
- The number jumps just because traffic grew. That means raw counts were compared instead of shares. Shares are each category's fraction of its own total.
- The gaps look odd because the categories in the two lists are in a different order. Then billing is being compared with refunds.

**Quickest check**

Run the weekly category-mix query from the lesson. Put those production shares next to your eval set's shares, one category per row. Look at the biggest gaps first. If the halved total of the gaps is well above zero, your eval set is out of date and needs refreshing.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where this simple check needs extra care.

**The mix holds steady, but the questions inside change.** "Billing" can stay at 50% while the billing questions shift to a brand-new product. Total variation distance only sees category shares, so it reports 0 drift. Also read a sample of real questions each week, or compare their **embeddings** (number lists that capture meaning) against your eval questions.

**Very little traffic.** With only 20 questions in a week, a few odd ones can swing the shares a lot and look like drift. Use a longer time window, and only act when the shift stays high for several windows in a row.

**Brand-new categories appear.** The measure assumes both lists share the same categories, so a new topic like "subscriptions" has no slot to land in. Keep an "other" bucket, watch its share closely, and add real examples of new topics to your eval set when it grows.

learn:term.a:
**They're the same thing.** In this lesson, "drift" is just the short name for "data drift." A third name, "distribution shift," means the same too.

All three describe one idea. The mix of real questions moves away from the mix in your eval set (your fixed set of test questions).

**Why two names?** "Drift" is quicker to say. "Data drift" is more precise. It tells you *what* moved: the incoming data, meaning the questions users ask. Your model didn't change. The world around it did.

**Everyday comparison:** Say you plan a café menu around last summer's orders: mostly iced coffee. Winter arrives and people want hot soup. Your menu didn't get worse. The customers' mix changed. Call it "drift" or "data drift." It's the same problem.

**The lesson's example:**

- Eval set: billing 50%, shipping 30%, refunds 20%
- Production: billing 20%, shipping 30%, refunds 50%

The gaps are 0.3 + 0 + 0.3 = 0.6. Halved, that's 0.3. This number is the total variation distance, which measures how far apart two mixes are. Whatever you call the shift, 0.3 is its size.

judge.notes: No major problem. The 'more precise' and 'your model didn't change' remarks go slightly beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Ship it: 4 points overall outweighs one case”?
check:0:0.a:
That option gets one thing right. Version B really is better on average. Going from 88% to 92% is a real gain, and you shouldn't throw that work away.

What it misses is what a must-pass set is for. Those 15 cases aren't ordinary questions. You picked them in the **Frame** stage because getting them wrong would be costly or embarrassing, like a fraud warning or a refund policy. So they aren't traded against the average. A gain on many everyday questions doesn't pay for one broken answer that matters most.

The average can't even show you the problem. A 92% score looks great while `fraud-03` quietly fails underneath. That's why the must-pass set is checked first and on its own, as a **release gate**. A release gate is a rule that blocks a release if any check fails. One failure means no ship, whatever the overall score says.

You don't have to drop B, though. Fix `fraud-03`, rerun the gate, then ship.

"It doesn't ship until that case passes" is better because it keeps B's gains but refuses to trade away the one answer that must never get worse.

judge.notes: Minor: it treats `fraud-03` as the failing case, which comes from the lesson's example rather than the Check question, and it doesn't define the "Frame stage".

check:0:1.q: Why not “Remove that question from the must-pass set”?
check:0:1.a:
Removing the question makes the gate pass, but it doesn't fix anything. Version B still gets the fraud case wrong. You've just stopped looking.

**What it gets right, a little:** a must-pass case can sometimes be wrong itself. Maybe the expected answer is outdated. Fixing a broken case is fine. But that's a careful decision about the case, made on its own. It shouldn't happen because a new version happened to fail it.

**What it misses:** the whole point of the set. You picked these cases in the **Frame** stage, before any experiment, because getting them wrong would be costly or embarrassing. Choosing them early means test results can't bend the rules later. Deleting a case the moment it fails is "moving the goalposts": changing the target so you look like you hit it. Do that a few times and the set protects nothing. A real customer could still get the bad fraud answer.

The 4-point gain on average doesn't change this. An average can hide one serious failure.

**Why "It doesn't ship until that case passes" is better:** it keeps the gate as a hard rule, so the answer that matters most can never quietly get worse.

judge.notes: No real problems; the 'fraud case' wording and the point about fixing an outdated case come from outside the quiz question, but they don't contradict the lesson.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Delete it, since the bug is fixed”?
check:1:0.a:
"Delete it" gets one thing right: the bug is fixed today. The new version gives the correct refund policy, so the problem feels finished.

What it misses is that fixes don't stay fixed on their own. Next month you might change the prompt, swap the model, or update the documents the bot reads. Any of those can quietly bring the old wrong answer back. That's called a **regression**: something that used to work breaks again.

If you delete the question, nothing is watching for that. A new version could score higher on average and still give the wrong refund policy. The average wouldn't show it, and you'd only find out when a customer complains.

The refund policy is exactly the kind of answer that's costly to get wrong. That's why the lesson says to add every serious production failure you fix. A failure that already happened once is proof it can happen.

Adding it to the must-pass set is better because every future version must pass it before it ships, so the old mistake can never slip back unnoticed.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Keep it in the dev set only”?
check:1:2.a:
Keeping the refund question in the **dev set** gets one thing right. The **dev set** is the pile of examples you test against while building and tweaking the bot, so the question stays around and still gets tested.

But it misses the main lesson. In the dev set, the refund question is just one case among hundreds. Its result gets blended into the overall average. Say a new version breaks the refund answer again but improves twenty other answers. The average goes up, and the version looks like a win. Nobody notices the old bug came back.

That is exactly the failure the lesson warns about: winning on average while breaking the answer that matters most. A wrong refund policy costs money and trust, so it can't be one vote among many.

The **must-pass set** treats it differently. It is checked first, on its own, apart from the overall score. If that case fails, the version doesn't ship, whatever its average says. That check is the **release gate**.

"Add it to the must-pass set" is better because a single failure on that question blocks the release, so the fixed bug can't quietly return.

judge.notes: No real problems. It adds small details the lesson doesn't give (the dev set definition, 'among hundreds'), but none of them contradict the lesson.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Halfway, once you see what passes”?
check:2:1.a:
"Halfway" gets one thing right. Running experiments teaches you a lot, and results can remind you of cases you forgot. That instinct helps later.

But choosing the set halfway has a hidden problem. Once you've seen what passes, the results bend your choices. Without meaning to, you might skip a hard case your current version fails, because including it would block you. Then the must-pass set protects your version, not your users.

The set should answer a different question: what would be costly or embarrassing to get wrong? A wrong refund policy. A missing fraud warning. That answer doesn't depend on any version's score.

You still add cases later. Every serious production failure (a real mistake users hit after release) goes in, so it can't come back. That's growing the list, not choosing it.

"At the start, before any experiment" is better because picking cases in the Frame stage (the first step, where you decide the question and what success means) keeps the release gate (the pass-or-block check before shipping) honest: it's set by what matters, not by what already passes.

check:2:2.q: Why not “At the end, just before you ship”?
check:2:2.a:
"At the end, just before you ship" gets one thing right. Ship is a moment when the must-pass set matters. The lesson says you check it there, as the release gate. So the timing of the *check* is partly correct.

What it misses is the timing of the *choice*. By the end, you've already seen how your versions behave. That knowledge leaks in, even if you don't mean it to. You might leave out the fraud case that version B now fails, because it feels like an edge case. Then the gate passes. It only passes because you drew the line around your results.

It also leaves the middle of the project unguarded. Without the set in place early, you can't check it during **Evaluate**. A version that breaks a critical answer could look like a winner for weeks.

The must-pass set should come from one question: "What would be costly or embarrassing to get wrong?" It shouldn't come from "What does our current version handle?"

Choosing at the start, before any experiment, is better because the cases are fixed by what matters to the business, before any result can bend your judgment.

judge.notes: No major problems. It is close to the length limit, uses 'edge case' without explaining it, and 'for weeks' is a small embellishment beyond the lesson.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Look up each must-pass case” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer you could say out loud:**

**The problem.** "An average score can hide a disaster. Version B might score 92% overall, beating A's 88%, and still get the fraud warning wrong. An average can't see which answers matter most."

**The idea.** "So I keep a small must-pass set. These are the cases that must never get worse, picked at the start of the project. Before I look at the overall score, I check each of them on its own. If even one fails, the version doesn't ship, whatever its average says. That's a release gate: a hard yes-or-no check before release."

**The trade-off.** "The set has to stay small and truly non-negotiable. If I stuff it with nice-to-have cases, the gate blocks every release and people start ignoring it."

**A likely follow-up:** *"How does a case get into the must-pass set?"*

**Hint at a strong answer:** Two routes. First, at the start, pick what would be costly or embarrassing to get wrong. Second, add every serious production failure you fix. That way an old bug can't quietly come back.

judge.notes: No blocking problems. Minor: the trade-off about people ignoring a bloated gate is not in the lesson, and the answer skips the lookup edge case that a missing case counts as failed.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- A new version scores higher on average, yet soon after release someone reports a wrong refund answer or a missing fraud warning. The average hid it.
- A failure you already fixed shows up again in production (real use by real users).
- Your release record shows only one overall score, with no separate must-pass result next to it.
- The must-pass set was picked late, after experiments began, instead of in Frame (the first project step, where you decide what success means). Late picks tend to miss what's truly costly.
- A must-pass case has no result for the new version, but the version shipped anyway. Not tested is not passed.

**Quickest check**

Take the version that's live now. List your must-pass case ids. For each one, find its result from the latest eval (the scoring run on your test cases). Any case that failed or has no result means the gate (the pass-or-block check before release) was skipped or ignored. Then compare your recent serious production failures to that list. Any that are missing still need adding.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three places where the must-pass gate needs extra care.

**1. LLM answers vary from run to run.** An LLM app can give a slightly different answer each time you ask. So a case might pass once and fail the next time, and a single run can fool you. Run each must-pass case several times, and count it as passing only if every run passes.

**2. The scorer is itself an LLM.** Often a second model, called an "LLM judge," grades the answers. That judge can be wrong too. It might block a good version or wave through a bad one. For must-pass cases, prefer strict checks, like "the answer must mention the fraud hotline." Have a person look at any failure before deciding.

**3. The right answer changes over time.** Policies get updated. Last year's correct refund answer may be wrong today. A stale case can then block a correct version. Give the set an owner, and review it whenever a policy changes. Keep the set small, so this review stays quick.

learn:term.a:
They are different kinds of things. **Frame** is a stage: the first step of a project, where you decide the question and what success means. A **must-pass set** is a thing you build: a small list of cases that can never get worse.

Frame is where the set starts. Before any experiment, you pick the cases that would be costly or embarrassing to get wrong. The set keeps growing after that. Every serious production failure you fix gets added, so it can't quietly come back.

The set is then used later, in **Evaluate** and **Ship**. It's checked first, apart from the overall score. One failure blocks the release. That block is the **release gate**.

Everyday comparison: planning a dinner party is Frame. That's when you write "no peanuts, a guest is allergic." That note is your must-pass set. If a guest later reacts to sesame, you add sesame too. A delicious menu still fails if one dish has peanuts.

The lesson's example: version B scores 92% against A's 88%. But must-pass case `fraud-03` fails, so B doesn't ship until it passes again.

judge.notes: No real problems found. The only minor point is that Evaluate and Ship are named without a short definition, but the answer stays under 200 words and everything it says matches the lesson.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Stop reviewing drafts: the drafter has earned t…”?
check:0:1.a:
"Stop reviewing drafts" gets one thing right. Experts changed only 2 of the last 150 drafts, so the drafter is doing well. The lesson says that is a good reason to send fewer drafts for review.

What it misses is that 2 out of 150 is not zero. Some drafts are still wrong. If one of those wrong drafts is on a **must-pass** question, it matters a lot. The lesson says those are the questions where a wrong label is costly. With no review at all, nobody would catch it.

Stopping also ends the tracking. The lesson says to keep watching how often experts change a draft. If no one checks any drafts, that number disappears. Then you can no longer tell whether the drafter still deserves trust.

So a low change rate earns *less* review, not *no* review.

"Review fewer drafts, but keep the riskiest in the queue" is better because it saves expert time while still checking the must-pass, disagreeing and rare-group drafts, and it keeps the change rate measurable.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Have experts rewrite every label from scratch a…”?
check:0:2.a:
Rewriting every label from scratch gets one thing right: an expert's own answer is the most trusted kind of label.

But look at the evidence. Here, an LLM (a large language model, the kind of AI behind chatbots) writes a first draft of each expected answer. This is called pre-labelling. Experts then confirm or fix each draft. They changed only 2 of the last 150. So the drafts are almost always right already.

Rewriting from scratch throws that work away. Checking a draft is several times faster than writing one. Experts would spend far more time for labels that are barely better. Expert time is the scarce part, and this wastes it.

It also ignores those 2 changes. Some drafts still go wrong, so keep checking where mistakes hurt most. One case is must-pass questions, which the app must always get right, so a wrong label is costly. Another is questions where two separate drafting attempts gave different answers, which hints the question is unclear.

"Review fewer drafts, but keep the riskiest in the queue" is better because it saves expert time where drafts are reliable and keeps checks where an error would cost the most.

check:1:0.q: Why not “A draft from a rare group”?
check:1:0.a:
"A draft from a rare group" is a reasonable instinct. It just isn't the top priority.

**What it gets right:** Rare groups do matter. A "group" is a category of questions, like `refund` or `fraud`. When a group has only a few questions, each label carries more weight. So one wrong label there skews your picture of how the app handles that group. That's why rare-group drafts are on the priority list at all.

**What it misses:** The lesson puts rare groups *third*. Must-pass questions come first, and drafts that disagree come second. In the scoring, a rare group earns just 1 point, while must-pass earns 4. You can see it in the example: `fraud-44` is from a rare group but only scores 1. `refund-02` is must-pass and scores 4, so it goes first.

With time for only one review, you spend it where a mistake hurts most. Rare groups are a tiebreaker-style boost, not the main signal.

**Why must-pass wins:** A must-pass question is one where a wrong label is costly, so it's the draft most worth an expert's single check.

judge.notes: Minor: calling the rare-group boost 'tiebreaker-style' is loose, since the lesson breaks ties by id, but it does not contradict the lesson.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The draft written most recently”?
check:1:2.a:
"The draft written most recently" sounds sensible, because new work feels fresh. But when a draft was written tells you nothing about how much a mistake in it would matter.

The lesson ranks drafts by risk, not by time. It looks at three things:

- Is it a **must-pass** question? A must-pass question is one where a wrong label is costly.
- Did two independent drafting runs **disagree**? That usually means the question is ambiguous.
- Is it from a **rare group**? Then each label carries more weight.

A recent draft might match none of these. If your expert spends their one check on it, a costly must-pass label could go unchecked. Expert time is the scarce part, so it should go where an error hurts most.

Sorting by recency is like a hospital seeing whoever walked in last. It ignores how urgent each case is.

A must-pass question's draft is the better answer because it is where a wrong label costs the most, so checking it first protects the most with the least expert time.

check:2:1.q: Why not “One drafting run crashed early”?
check:2:1.a:
It's a fair guess. Software does sometimes fail partway, so a broken run is possible. But it's not what disagreement *usually* means.

The question says both runs gave expected facts, and the facts differ. "Expected facts" are the key points a correct answer should contain. A crash is a one-off fault in the process. It says nothing about the question itself. So it misses the more common and more useful reason.

That reason is the question. When two independent drafting runs read the same question and the same source article and still land on different facts, the question can often be read more than one way. That is why the lesson ranks disagreement as a reason to review. It sits second, after must-pass questions (the ones where a wrong label is costly).

"The question is probably ambiguous" is better because it names the usual cause of disagreement, and that cause is exactly what a human expert can settle.

check:2:2.q: Why not “The source article is too short”?
check:2:2.a:
It's a fair guess, and it isn't completely wrong. A short article might leave gaps. Two drafting runs could then fill those gaps differently. A "drafting run" is one pass where the LLM reads the question and its source article and writes the expected facts.

But article length isn't the usual cause. Even a long, detailed article can produce two different drafts if the question can be read in more than one way. In that case, each run picks a different reading and pulls different facts to match it. The article isn't the problem. The question is.

That's why the lesson ranks disagreeing drafts second in the review queue, right after must-pass questions. When the drafts don't match, someone has to decide which reading the question really means. Only an expert can make that call. A longer article wouldn't settle it.

"The question is probably ambiguous" is the better answer because it names the most common cause of disagreement. That cause is a question with more than one sensible meaning, and that is exactly the kind of draft an expert needs to see.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Score, then sort” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "Experts only have time to check some of the LLM-drafted labels. So we need to choose which drafts they see first."

*The idea:* "Give each item points for risk signals. Must-pass questions, two drafting runs that disagree, and rare groups each add points. Then sort, highest first, and review from the top until time runs out. Ties go in A to Z order by id, so the queue is the same every run."

*Edge case:* "Low-scoring items aren't ignored. We spot-check some. We also track how often experts change drafts. That tells us whether to review more or fewer."

**Likely follow-up:** "Why use points instead of a fixed rule order?"

*Hint:* Be honest first. With weights 4, 2 and 1, each weight is bigger than all the smaller ones added together. So points give exactly the same order as a fixed rule order. The real gain is flexibility. Change one number, and two smaller signals together can outrank one bigger signal. Adding a new signal means adding one weight, not rewriting the rules.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Scores look too good, then drop in real use.** This often means the drafter saw the app's own answer. The "expected facts" then just echo the app, so the app grades itself as right.
- **Experts almost never change a draft.** That can be good news. It can also mean they are rubber-stamping, which means clicking "confirm" without really reading.
- **Experts change most drafts.** The drafting prompt is weak. Review is no faster than writing from scratch.
- **Failures cluster in must-pass or rare-group questions.** The review order was likely skipped, so the riskiest labels were never checked.
- **Two drafting runs disagree, yet the label was accepted unreviewed.** An ambiguous question slipped through.

**Quickest check**

Take about ten confirmed labels, mostly must-pass ones. Ask an expert to write the expected facts fresh, without seeing the draft. Compare them with the confirmed labels. Big gaps mean the review is not catching errors.

Then open the drafter's inputs in a few traces. A trace is the saved record of each step. Confirm the app's answer was never passed to the drafter.

judge.notes: No real problems. The line 'Review is no faster than writing from scratch' slightly overstates the lesson's point that the prompt needs work before it saves time.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Both drafts agree, but both are wrong.** If the two drafting runs use the same model and prompt, they can share the same blind spot, so "agree" does not mean "correct." Use two different models or prompts for the runs, and spot-check a sample of the agreeing drafts too.

**2. Experts get too trusting.** Seeing a draft first can pull an expert toward accepting it. This is called **anchoring**, and it means a low change rate might reflect tired reviewers rather than good drafts. To tell the difference, slip in a few drafts with known, planted mistakes and see whether experts catch them.

**3. The source articles change over time.** A label confirmed last month can go stale when the refund policy or billing article is updated. Record which version of the article each label came from, and send labels back into the queue whenever their article changes.

learn:term.q: How is “drafts” different from “confirm or correct”?
learn:term.a:
They are two steps in one job: producing the **expected facts** for each question. Expected facts are the points a correct answer must contain.

**Drafting** is the first step. An LLM reads the question and its source article, then writes a first guess at the expected facts. It never sees the app's own answer, so the draft can't simply copy the app's mistakes. In MLflow, each draft is saved with `source_id="drafter-v1"`, so everyone can see a model wrote it.

**Confirming or correcting** is the second step. An expert reads the draft. If it's right, they confirm it. If it's wrong or missing something, they fix it. Only then does the label count as trusted.

Think of a new assistant drafting a reply letter. The manager reads it and either signs it or edits it first. Editing is much quicker than writing from a blank page.

In the lesson's example, `refund-02` is a must-pass question. So its draft goes to an expert first. A wrong label there would be costly. Drafts like `shipping-08` can wait or be spot-checked.

judge.notes: No real problems; a few small extras (the reason the drafter never sees the app's answer, and 'only then does the label count as trusted') go slightly beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Retrieval settings, like how many articles are …”?
check:0:0.a:
That option points at the wrong half of the pipeline for this bucket.

It does get one thing right. Retrieval settings, like how many articles are found, are a real cause of changes. They are worth checking, just for the other bucket, "retrieval differed".

What it misses is what the "same articles, different answer" bucket already tells you. Both versions sent the same set of articles to the model. Retrieval did its job identically each time, so its settings can't explain why the answer changed. If you had changed how many articles are found, the sets would likely differ, and the question would have landed in the "retrieval differed" bucket instead.

So the traces have ruled retrieval out. The change must have happened after the articles were handed over.

"The generation step, where the answer is written" is the better answer because, with the inputs held equal, only that step is left to blame: the prompt (the instructions given to the model), the model itself, or the scorer (the check that grades the answer).

judge.notes: Minor overstatement: "Retrieval did its job identically" ignores that the same set can arrive in a different order, as in the lesson's refund-11 example. It still matches the lesson's point that same articles means look at generation.

check:0:1.q: Why not “The eval set, since it may be too small to trust”?
check:0:1.a:
It's a fair worry in general. A small eval set (the list of test questions you score each version on) can make results noisy, so a few changes might be luck. Keeping that in mind is healthy.

But it doesn't answer the question asked. The bucket already tells you *where* things changed. "Same articles, different answer" means both versions found the same help articles and passed them to the model. So retrieval (the step that finds articles) behaved the same. Something after that point made the answers differ.

Blaming the eval set skips over that clue. Its size doesn't explain why identical inputs produced different answers. It's a general doubt that could be raised about any result. It doesn't point you to any part of the pipeline.

The lesson's point is that bucketing tells you which part to inspect. Here, that part is the one that comes after the articles are chosen. That means the prompt, the model, or the scorer (the check that grades each answer).

"The generation step, where the answer is written" is better because the articles were the same, so the only thing left that could have changed the answer is what happened after retrieval.

check:1:0.q: Why not “The prompt that writes the answer”?
check:1:0.a:
The prompt is a real suspect. It's just not the first one here.

What it gets right: the prompt can change an answer. When both versions send the same articles to the generation step (where the model writes the answer), the cause is somewhere in generation. That could be the prompt, the model or the scorer (the check that grades the answer).

What it misses: in this regression, the articles themselves changed. The model was handed different material to write from. Changing the inputs can change the answer even if the prompt is untouched. So if you start with the prompt, you might tweak wording that was never the problem. Meanwhile the real issue, wrong or missing articles, stays in place.

The trace already gave you the clue. Different articles means the change starts before generation, so look upstream (earlier in the pipeline) first.

"Retrieval: how articles are found" is better because the different articles point straight at the step that picks them, which is the earliest place the two versions split.

judge.notes: Minor overreach: it calls the issue 'wrong or missing articles' and retrieval 'the earliest place' the versions split, which the lesson doesn't state, but nothing contradicts the lesson.

check:1:2.q: Why not “The scorer that grades the answer”?
check:1:2.a:
It's a fair guess. The scorer can cause changes. The lesson even lists it as a suspect. But it belongs to the other bucket.

**What it gets right:** A scorer is the step that grades each answer. If it grades differently, results can flip even when nothing else changed. That's a real cause worth checking.

**What it misses:** This regression is in the "retrieval differed" bucket. The traces show the new version handed the model *different articles*. That is the earliest point where the two versions split. Everything after it, including the answer and the grade, depends on those articles. Give the model different source material and a different answer is expected. The scorer just grades what it receives.

You suspect the scorer when the articles were the *same* but the result changed anyway. Then retrieval is ruled out. What's left is the prompt, the model or the scorer.

**Why "Retrieval: how articles are found" is better:** The traces show the articles changed, so you start with the step that picks them. That is the first place the two versions differ.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Read all 60 in the order they appear”?
check:2:0.a:
Reading all 60 in order has one thing going for it: you won't skip anything. Every changed question gets looked at.

But it costs a lot and teaches you less than you'd expect.

**It eats the afternoon.** Each case means opening a trace (the step-by-step record of one run), comparing two answers, and judging what went wrong. Sixty of those can easily fill your whole afternoon, or more.

**The order is random.** Questions appear in whatever order the comparison listed them. Cases with the same cause end up scattered, so patterns are hard to spot.

**Much of it is repeat work.** Many changes share one cause. After the fifth case where the new version found worse articles, the next ten tell you little new.

**It doesn't point anywhere.** You finish with sixty notes but no clear split between "retrieval broke" (the search for help articles) and "generation broke" (the model writing the answer).

"Sort them into buckets, read a few of each" is the right answer. The traces sort the cases for free, so a small sample from each bucket shows you the causes and which part of the pipeline each one belongs to.

judge.notes: No blocking problem. Minor nits: it calls the order 'random' and gives a '5th case / next ten' figure, neither of which is in the lesson, and the closing 'one sentence' is really two.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Read the 5 newest and skip the rest”?
check:2:1.a:
**Why not "Read the 5 newest and skip the rest"?**

It gets one thing right. You can't read all 60 in an afternoon, so reading only a few is sensible.

The problem is *which* few. "Newest" just means most recent. It has nothing to do with why a result changed. Your 5 could all come from one kind of change, for example all from questions where the articles differed. You'd miss the questions where the articles stayed the same but the answer changed anyway. You'd also have no idea how the other 55 split, so you couldn't tell whether retrieval (finding articles) or generation (writing the answer) deserves your attention.

**Why "Sort them into buckets, read a few of each" is better:** a quick automatic check first splits all 60 into "different articles" (points at retrieval) and "same articles" (points at generation: the prompt, the model or the scorer). Then reading a few from each bucket means both parts of the pipeline get looked at before you label causes.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Compare as sets, then bucket” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "A comparison over a few hundred questions can flag sixty changed results. That's too many to read one by one."

*The idea:* "So I sort them first, straight from the traces. A trace is the recorded log of each step a request went through. For each changed question, I take the articles each version sent to the generation step, where the model writes the answer. I compare them as sets, meaning order and repeats don't matter. Different sets go in a retrieval bucket. The same sets go in a generation bucket, which points at the prompt, the model or the scorer. Then I read a handful from each bucket and label causes."

*The trade-off:* "I only read a sample per bucket, so a rare cause can slip past. In return, I get the error analysis for a fraction of the reading, and each cause is already tied to one part of the pipeline."

**A likely follow-up**

"Which articles do you compare if the pipeline has a reranker?" A reranker is a step that reorders and trims the retrieved list.

*Hint:* Compare what actually reached generation. That means the reranker's output if it exists, and the retriever's output otherwise.

judge.notes: No real problems. It runs close to 200 words, and the 'rare cause can slip past' trade-off is a sensible inference rather than something the lesson states.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **Almost everything lands in "retrieval differed."** Often the lists were compared in order, not as sets. A question like `refund-11`, with the same three articles reshuffled, gets put in the wrong bucket.
- **The "same articles" bucket is empty even after a prompt change.** A prompt edit should usually leave some questions with identical articles but new answers.
- **Fixes don't stick.** You tune retrieval, yet the regressions stay. The real cause was in generation (the step where the model writes the answer).
- **Buckets don't match the traces.** If your pipeline has a reranker (a step that re-orders and trims the found articles), but you read the retriever's output instead, you are bucketing the wrong article list.
- **You're still reading all sixty changes one by one.** The sorting step was skipped.

**Quickest check**

Pick three rows from each bucket and compare the two lists by eye, ignoring order. In "same articles," both lists should hold exactly the same IDs. In "retrieval differed," at least one ID should appear in only one of the lists. That covers an article added, and also one simply dropped.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The model is random.** Many models give slightly different answers to the same input, even when nothing changed. Those questions land in the "same articles, different answer" bucket and look like generation problems. Before comparing, run each question a few times on the old version, and set aside any whose answer changes on its own.

**2. Two parts changed at once.** Suppose the new version has a new retriever (the search step) and a new prompt. A question whose articles differ goes under retrieval, but the new prompt may be what changed its answer. Change one part at a time, or rerun the new prompt with the old articles to see which change mattered.

**3. Articles arrive more than once.** An agent (a program where the model decides its own steps) may search several times before answering. The lesson's helper reads only the first search step (`steps[0]`), so it can miss later articles. Gather the articles from every search step before comparing.

judge.notes: The answer is sound. The only blemish is the inline `steps[0]` reference, which sits slightly against the 'no code' instruction, but it is a name, not code.

learn:term.a:
They aren't two of the same kind of thing. "Different articles" is a **clue** you read from the traces. "Generation" is a **step** in the pipeline.

**Generation** is the step where the model reads the articles it was handed and writes the answer.

**Different articles** describes what reached that step. Before generation, retrieval (the search step) picks help articles. If the old and new versions handed over different sets, the change most likely started in retrieval.

They work together as a two-way test:

- **Different articles**: the input to generation changed. Look at retrieval first.
- **Same articles, different answer**: the input was identical, yet the output changed. So the cause sits inside generation: the prompt, the model, or the scorer (the thing grading the answer).

Think of a cook. If the shopping bag held different ingredients, blame the shopping. If the bag was the same and the dish still changed, blame the cooking.

In the lesson's example, `billing-06` got `kb-04` and `kb-09` instead of `kb-12` and `kb-02`, so its bag changed. `refund-11` got the same three articles, only reordered. So something changed in the cooking.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Nothing: each split keeps the same share of que…”?
check:0:0.a:
That option gets one thing right. If you re-deal all 300 by position, each split still gets the same share. Dev still has 60%, test 20%, holdout 20%. On paper, nothing looks broken.

What it misses is *which* questions land where. Dealing by position means a question's split depends on where it sits in the list. Add 100 new questions, and the positions shift. Old questions get shuffled into different splits.

That matters most for the holdout. The holdout is the set you keep locked away and only check at the end, so it gives an honest score. Suppose a question you tuned your agent on in dev now moves into the holdout. Your agent has already "seen" it, so it does well there. The holdout score goes up, but not because the agent got better. That is the quiet inflation the lesson warns about.

The right sizes don't help if the wrong questions are inside them.

"Old questions can move, even into the holdout" is better because it names the real danger: questions changing splits and leaking into the set that is meant to stay untouched.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The 100 new questions all land in the dev set”?
check:0:2.a:
**Why "The 100 new questions all land in the dev set" isn't the best answer**

It looks at the wrong questions. Where the *new* questions land isn't the danger. They are fresh, so they're fine in any split.

It's also not what happens. Say the deal is "first 60% to dev, next 20% to test, last 20% to holdout," and the 100 new questions go on the end. Out of 300, the cut points move. Dev now runs to position 180, test to 240, holdout to 300. So the new questions (positions 201 to 300) land in test and holdout, not dev.

What it misses is that the *old* questions move. In the same example, old test and old holdout questions slide into dev. Your holdout is no longer untouched. And re-dealing often means shuffling first. Then any old question can land anywhere, including a dev question you tuned on landing in the holdout. That makes the holdout score look better than it really is.

**Why "Old questions can move, even into the holdout" is better:** it names the real risk, which is that re-dealing by position shuffles questions you've already used, so your splits stop being trustworthy.

judge.notes: It flatly says the new questions do not land in dev, based on an assumed append-only 60/20/20 deal the lesson never states, then adds an unsupported claim that re-dealing often shuffles first, where any question can land anywhere, which contradicts that flat claim.

check:1:1.q: Why not “They get dealt out again”?
check:1:1.a:
"They get dealt out again" describes the **old** method, not the hashing one. If you dealt questions by position (first 60% to dev, and so on), adding 100 new questions would shift everyone's position. Old questions could then change splits. A question you tuned on might land in the holdout and make its score look better than it really is.

Hashing works differently. A **hash** turns text, like an id, into a number. The same text always gives the same number. You take the remainder after dividing by 100 (`% 100`) to get a bucket from 0 to 99. The bucket decides the split.

The key point is that the bucket depends on the id **alone**. It ignores how many questions exist and where each one sits in the list. So `"ticket-1001"` gets bucket 72 and goes to test today, next week, and a year from now. The 100 new questions get their own buckets. Nothing old gets touched.

"They stay in the same split" is better because each split comes only from the question's own id, so adding new questions cannot move old ones.

check:1:2.q: Why not “They all move into dev”?
check:1:2.a:
"They all move into dev" gets one thing right: it takes seriously the worry that adding questions could disturb old ones. That worry is real when you deal questions out by position. Change the list, and old questions can land somewhere new.

But hashing removes that worry. A **hash** is a function that turns text, like an id, into a big number. The same id always gives the same number. Your split then comes from that number alone. You take the remainder after dividing by 100 (`% 100`), which gives a bucket from 0 to 99. Under 60 is dev, 60 to 79 is test, and 80 to 99 is holdout.

Notice what is missing from that rule. It never looks at the other questions or at how many there are. So new questions can't change an old question's bucket. `"ticket-1001"` gave 72 last week, and it gives 72 today. It stays in test.

Nothing in the rule pushes questions toward dev, either. Each id lands wherever its own number says.

"They stay in the same split" is better because each question's split depends only on its own id, and that id never changes.

judge.notes: The second paragraph spells out the whole stable_split recipe in order (hash the id, take % 100, then the 0-59 / 60-79 / 80-99 ranges), which the question did not need and which hands over the exercise's logic.

check:2:0.a:
Hashing the question text does get one thing right. The same text always gives the same number, so a question won't move between splits as long as its text never changes.

But it misses the real problem. The conversation has 5 questions, and each one has different text. Different text gives different numbers, which means different buckets (the 0 to 99 slot that decides the split). So the 5 questions still scatter across dev, test and holdout. That is the same leak you had with question ids. The model can tune on part of a conversation and then be tested on the rest of it.

The text also has a weakness of its own. If someone fixes a typo or rewords a question, its hash changes and it can jump to a different split. That breaks the "splits that don't move" promise.

**The conversation id** is better because every question in that conversation shares it, so all 5 hash to the same bucket and land in one split together.

check:2:2.q: Why not “The date it was asked”?
check:2:2.a:
The date has one thing going for it. It never changes, so hashing it gives the same bucket every time. Questions from the same day would always land together.

But the leakage rule isn't about days. It's about conversations. Leakage means the same conversation shows up in two splits, so the model gets tested on something it was tuned on. The date doesn't line up with that.

- **A conversation can cross days.** A customer might start at 11:58 pm and finish after midnight, or come back on Tuesday. Those questions get different dates, different buckets, and possibly different splits. The leak is back.
- **It lumps unrelated conversations together.** Every conversation from one day goes to the same split. A busy day, or a day with an outage, could fill up the holdout with one topic. Your splits get lopsided.
- **There are few dates.** A month has only about 30 dates. So the 60/20/20 split works out only roughly, depending on which days happen to land where.

The conversation id is better because it is exactly the thing you want kept together. Every question in a conversation shares it, so they all land in one split.

judge.notes: The answer is sound. It is close to the word limit, and the closing 'one sentence' is really two, but neither is serious.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Turn the id into a bucket” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "Our eval set grows every week. If we re-deal questions into dev, test and holdout by position, old questions move. A question we tuned on could slip into the holdout and make our scores look better than they are."

*The idea:* "So we decide each question's split from its id alone. A hash turns the id into a big number, and the same id always gives the same number. We take the remainder after dividing by 100 to get a bucket from 0 to 99. Under 60 goes to dev, 60 to 79 to test, and the rest to holdout. New questions never disturb old ones."

*The edge case:* "Hash the right id. If one conversation has several questions, hash the conversation id, so they all land together and nothing leaks across splits."

**A likely follow-up**

"Why not just shuffle with a fixed random seed?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* A seed (a starting number that makes the shuffle repeatable) only repeats the shuffle for the same list. Add one question and every position shifts, so old questions move. Also mention that changing the hash function or the 60/80 cut-offs would move items too, so lock both in early.

judge.notes: No real problems. The seed follow-up goes slightly beyond the lesson, and 'every position shifts' is loose for items added at the end. The total is about 207 words, but the spoken part is only about 140.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **A question changes split.** Last week `ticket-1001` was in test. This week it shows up in holdout. That should never happen. It means splits are being re-dealt by position, not decided from the id.
- **Holdout scores look too good, then real use disappoints.** If questions you tuned on slide into holdout, the holdout (the set you save for a final, honest check) quietly gets easier. The score rises, but real users don't see the gain.
- **One conversation sits in two splits.** You find the same `conversation_id` in both dev and test. That breaks the leakage rule. It usually means the question id was hashed (turned into a number) instead of the conversation id.

**Quickest check**

Keep last week's list of each id and its split. Compare it with this week's list. For every id in both lists, the split should match exactly. Even one difference means splits are moving.

Then group the table by `conversation_id` and count how many different splits each one has. Every count should be 1. Anything higher means a conversation's questions were split apart.

learn:stops.a:
**1. You change the hash or the percentages.** The promise "same id, same split" only holds if the recipe never changes. Switching to a different hash function, or moving from 60/20/20 to 70/15/15, reshuffles old questions. Pick the recipe once, write it down, and store the `split` column on the table so old rows keep their label.

**2. The set is very small.** A hash spreads ids out evenly only on average. With 30 questions, the holdout might get 2 or 9 instead of 6. Always count each split after assigning. For tiny sets, it is fine to assign splits by hand and then freeze them.

**3. Your data changes over time.** Hashing mixes old and new questions evenly into every split. That is a problem if users now ask about a new product your app never saw. If you want to know how the app handles what is coming next, also keep a time-based holdout: the newest few weeks of questions, kept aside and never tuned on.

judge.notes: No real problems; the second situation runs to four sentences rather than two or three, which is minor.

learn:term.a:
They answer two different questions.

**"Id alone"** is the rule. It says *what* decides a question's split: only its id. Not its position in the list, not how many questions exist, not when it was added. Since nothing else feeds in, adding new questions can't move an old one.

**A hash** is the tool. It is a function that turns text like `"ticket-1001"` into a big number. The same text always gives the same number. Then `% 100` (the remainder after dividing by 100) shrinks that number to a bucket from 0 to 99.

How they fit: the rule says "use only the id." The hash is how you turn that id into a bucket, and the bucket picks the split.

Everyday comparison: a post office sorts letters by the last two digits of the house number. "Look only at the address" is the rule. "Read the last two digits" is the method. A new street built nearby doesn't change where your letter goes.

In the lesson's example, `"ticket-1001"` lands in bucket 72, so it goes to test. A month and 500 new questions later, it's still 72, still test.

check:0:1.q: Why not “The plain eval-set average, since every example…”?
check:0:1.a:
"Every example counts once" sounds fair, and it gets one thing right. It is an honest summary of **the eval set itself**. If you only asked "how did we do on these test questions?", it would be the answer.

But the eval set is not a copy of real traffic. You chose to give refunds extra examples, 3 in 10, so you could measure them properly. Real users only ask about refunds 1 in 20 times. A plain average counts refunds about six times more than users actually meet them. Because refunds score badly, the headline looks **worse** than what real users experience.

It also hides something. One blended number never shows that refunds are the weak spot. Billing could be fine and refunds broken, and you would only see a vague middle score.

"Weighted" just means each group counts in proportion to its share of real traffic.

**The traffic-weighted score, shown next to each group's score, is better because the headline matches what real users experience, while the per-group scores keep the refunds problem in plain sight.**

check:0:2.q: Why not “The refund score alone, since it is the worst”?
check:0:2.a:
Picking the worst score gets one thing right: it refuses to let a bad group hide. Refunds failing is a real problem, and you should not bury it.

But as the overall number, it misleads. Refunds are only 1 in 20 of real questions. The refund score tells you nothing about how the other 19 in 20 questions go. So the headline would describe a small slice of traffic as if it were all of it.

It also throws information away. The other groups' scores, and how many examples each one rests on, disappear from the report.

A plain average of the eval set has the opposite flaw. Refunds are 3 in 10 of your eval examples. That is right for measuring them closely. But averaging that way makes refunds count six times more than they do in real traffic.

"The traffic-weighted score, shown next to each group's score" is better because the headline counts each group as often as real questions do, while the per-group scores keep the refund problem in plain view.

check:1:0.q: Why not “The same 90 percent, but in bold”?
check:1:0.a:
Making the number bold changes how it looks, not what it says. The manager asked a specific question: are refund questions working? A single 90 percent can't answer that, however loudly you print it.

Is there anything right about it? Only that a headline number is useful. A quick summary has its place. But the problem was never that the number was hard to see. The problem is that one overall score blends every group together. Billing could be passing almost every time while refunds fail half the time, and the blend can still land at a comfortable 90 percent. The weak group hides inside the strong one.

Bold also adds false confidence. It makes the number look more important, which makes the hidden problem easier to miss.

"A score for each group, with its count" is better because it shows the refund score on its own. The count tells the manager how many examples that score rests on, so they know how much to trust it.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Last week's score next to it”?
check:1:1.a:
"Last week's score next to it" does get one thing right. It shows a **trend**, meaning whether things got better or worse over time. That is useful. If the score dropped from 95% to 90%, you would know something changed.

But it answers a different question. The manager asked about **refunds**. Two overall numbers still mix every group together. Refunds could be failing half the time in both weeks, and both numbers would still look fine because billing is so large.

It can even hide a fresh problem. Say billing improved a little and refunds got much worse in the same week. The two changes can cancel out. The overall score stays flat, and nobody notices that refunds broke.

So you would still not be able to say "refunds are working" or "refunds are not." You would only know the blend moved, or did not.

"A score for each group, with its count" is better because it answers the manager directly: you can point to the refunds number and see how many examples it rests on, so you know how much to trust it.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Give it a score of zero”?
check:2:0.a:
"Give it a score of zero" gets one thing right. It refuses to pretend the gift card group is fine. Something real is missing, and a zero at least makes noise about it.

But a score is a claim about evidence. A zero says "we tested gift card questions and every single one failed." You never tested any. The honest number of examples behind that group is zero. That means you know nothing about it, not that it fails.

Treating "unknown" as "failing" causes two problems:

- **It distorts the headline.** If gift cards get some share of real traffic, a fake 0% drags the weighted score down for a failure that may not exist.
- **It points to the wrong fix.** A zero invites people to debug the agent. The actual gap is in your eval set, which simply has no gift card questions yet.

"Call it a blind spot to fill" is better because it reports the truth (no data yet) and names the right next step: write gift card examples, then measure that group for real.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Leave it out, since it's new”?
check:2:2.a:
**"Leave it out, since it's new" gets one thing right.** You have no gift card examples, so you can't give that group a score. Leaving it out at least avoids making up a number or logging it as 0%. A zero would wrongly say "it always fails" when really you just don't know.

**But it misses the bigger point.** Real users are already asking about gift cards. Being new doesn't make that traffic matter less. If the group simply vanishes from the report, three things go wrong:

- The report looks complete when it isn't. Readers assume every kind of question was checked.
- Your headline weighted score quietly covers only part of real traffic. Nobody can see which part is missing.
- Nothing prompts anyone to add gift card examples, so the gap can last for a long time.

In short, leaving it out hides the problem instead of reporting it.

**"Call it a blind spot to fill" is the better answer.** It openly flags that real users are meeting something you haven't measured, and it turns that gap into a clear next step: add gift card examples to the eval set.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “A weighted average” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
Here's a 30-second answer you could say out loud.

**The problem.** "One overall score can hide failures. Billing might pass 90% of the time while refunds pass only 50%. A plain average of the eval set, meaning my collection of test examples, counts each group by how many examples I wrote. It doesn't count how often real users hit that group."

**The idea.** "So the headline number is a weighted average. Each group counts as much as its share of real traffic. In my example, a plain average says 70%. Weighted by traffic it's 78%, because billing is 70% of what users ask."

**The edge case.** "A weighted headline can bury a small group that's failing. So I always report each group's score next to it, with how many examples it's based on. And if a group appears in traffic but not in my eval set, that's a blind spot, not a zero."

**Likely follow-up:** "Why not just make the eval set match traffic?"

*Hint:* Small groups would then get too few examples to measure reliably. Give them extra examples so you can measure them well. Then weight by traffic for the headline.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **One number only.** Your MLflow run shows a single `pass_rate` and no `pass_rate.billing` or `pass_rate.refunds`. You can't see which group is failing.
- **Good score, unhappy users.** The headline looks fine, but complaints cluster around one topic, such as refunds. A strong group was hiding a weak one.
- **Score shifts after launch.** The eval score is noticeably higher or lower than what real use shows. A common cause is a plain average. Your small groups got extra examples, so they count more than real users meet them.
- **Missing groups.** Real traffic contains a group that isn't in your eval set at all. That's a blind spot, not a zero.
- **Tiny counts.** A group shows 100% from just three examples. That score is shaky.

**Quickest check**

Put a small table side by side for each group: pass rate, number of eval examples, and share of real traffic. Then compute the plain average and the traffic-weighted average. If they differ a lot, or a traffic group has no eval examples, you've found the problem.

judge.notes: No significant problems; it is about 175 words and consistent with the lesson, though 'you've found the problem' when the two averages differ is slightly loose.

learn:stops.a:
Here are three situations where the rule needs extra care.

**A group has very few examples.** If refunds has only 5 eval examples, its pass rate can swing a lot from one run to the next just by chance. Always show the example count next to each score. Add more examples before trusting a big change in a small group.

**Traffic changes over time.** The traffic shares are a snapshot. If a product launch doubles refund questions, last month's shares make the headline number misleading. Recompute the shares regularly from recent logs (records of real user requests). The drift lesson later in this module covers how to notice this.

**Groups are fuzzy in an LLM app.** In a chatbot, one question can be about billing and refunds at once, or fit no group at all. Then the shares may not add up cleanly, and some traffic lands nowhere. Add an "other" group and label a sample of real questions by hand. Treat any traffic you can't score as a blind spot, not a zero.

learn:term.q: What does “for each group” mean here?
learn:term.a:
**"For each group"** means you split your test examples into categories and give each category its own score. You don't squash everything into one number.

**An everyday comparison:** a restaurant has an average rating of 4 stars. That sounds fine. Now rate each dish separately. The pizza gets 5 stars and the soup gets 2. The single average hid the soup problem. Rating each dish shows you exactly what to fix.

**In the lesson's example,** the groups are the kinds of questions users ask: `billing` and `refunds`. Every example in the eval set (the test questions you run your agent on) belongs to one group. So you report `billing` at 90% and `refunds` at 50%, each based on 50 examples.

The example count matters too. A score from 5 examples is much shakier than one from 50.

**In the MLflow code,** the loop saves one metric per group, such as `pass_rate.billing` and `pass_rate.refunds`. A metric is just a named number stored with the run. The weighted headline score, `pass_rate.weighted`, is saved separately. So you get both the big picture and the details.

judge.notes: No real problems; the restaurant analogy's numbers (average 4 with a 5 and a 2) are loose but not wrong.
